coverage: All twelve stories in both final live editions: named clients, households, police, culprits, aliases and disguise names, named references and principal unnamed figures. Story-scoped bindings; concealed identities, culprits and outcomes gated at paragraph end. Pronouns, generic descriptions and Holmes’s disguises unbound.
coordinateBase: chapters are stories 1-12; after uses one-based chapters and zero-based paragraph indices

entities.name: Sherlock Holmes
entities.subtitle: The consulting detective
entities.body: A private consulting detective with rooms in Baker Street, London. Clients bring him problems the police cannot solve or will not touch; his friend Dr. Watson narrates the cases.

aliasRules.why: Holmes’s signature on the pips he sends.

entities.notes: Disguises (the groom and clergyman in story 1, the old man in the opium den in story 6, the loafer in story 11) and descriptions of Holmes are deliberately unbound.

entities.name: Dr. Watson
entities.subtitle: Holmes’s friend and the narrator
entities.body: A doctor and Holmes’s friend, who narrates these cases. He shared rooms with Holmes at Baker Street before his marriage; some cases date from those bachelor days, others from after he returned to medical practice.
entities.notes: Watson is called “James” by his wife at 6:8; the name conflicts with no other figure but is left unbound and recorded as a source inconsistency. “Doctor” binds only in reviewed stories/paragraphs; in story 8 “the Doctor” is Roylott.

entities.name: Mrs. Hudson
entities.subtitle: Of the Baker Street household
entities.body: The woman who keeps house at Holmes’s Baker Street rooms and sees to his meals. Holmes jokes that he should have her check his dinner’s woodcock for jewels.

snapshots.body: The woman who keeps house at Holmes’s Baker Street rooms. She answers the door to early callers and has lit the fire for Holmes’s new client.
snapshots.why: Her part at 8:2–7.

entities.notes: The text of this collection never calls her landlady; story 1’s landlady is Mrs. Turner (separate entity). “Hudson” in 5:87 is a man in Elias Openshaw’s diary.

entities.name: Irene Adler
entities.subtitle: Opera singer; ‘the woman’ to Holmes
entities.body: A retired American-born opera singer living in London. Watson says she is the one woman Holmes always calls ‘the woman’, though not out of love.

aliasRules.why: Holmes asks the King for ‘Mademoiselle’s address’; unambiguously Irene Adler.
‘Miss Irene, or Madame, rather’ — Holmes correcting her title after the wedding (141).
Her letter’s signature ‘IRENE NORTON, née ADLER’; marriage already revealed at 141, letter is the reveal paragraph itself.

snapshots.body: An American-born contralto, born in New Jersey in 1858, once prima donna of the Imperial Opera of Warsaw and now retired and living in London. The King of Bohemia, who calls her a well-known adventuress, met her in Warsaw some five years ago, became entangled with her, and wants back the compromising letters he wrote her.
snapshots.why: 59–61: the King names her as his former acquaintance; Holmes’s index gives her biography and states the compromising letters.

snapshots.body: An American-born contralto, formerly prima donna of the Imperial Opera of Warsaw, now living at Briony Lodge, St. John’s Wood. She holds a compromising photograph of herself with the King of Bohemia. She has just married the lawyer Godfrey Norton in a hurried ceremony at the Church of St. Monica, with Holmes, in his groom’s disguise, pulled in as witness.
snapshots.why: 141: Holmes recounts the wedding of ‘Irene Adler, spinster, to Godfrey Norton, bachelor’.

snapshots.body: An American-born opera singer who outwits Holmes. She saw through his clergyman act after the fire alarm, followed him home in men’s clothes to wish him good night, and left England with her new husband, Godfrey Norton. In her letter, signed ‘Irene Norton, née Adler’, she promises not to trouble the King, keeping the photograph only for her own protection.
snapshots.why: 237 (flight) and 242–246 (her letter: male costume, the good-night at Baker Street, the promise, the signature).

entities.notes: Para 0 calls her ‘the late Irene Adler’ in both editions; this story does not say she has died and the card must not assert it. Watson keeps the name ‘Irene Adler’ after the marriage (185: ‘as I will still call her’), so the display name stays Irene Adler. ‘_the_ woman’ (0, 258) and ‘the woman’ (M 244) are left unbound. ‘Adler’ alone occurs only inside the bound phrases (and as uppercase ‘ADLER’ at 246), so it is not a separate alias. The youth in an ulster (213) is her in disguise but is a separate entity (youth-in-ulster), gated to 243.

entities.name: King of Bohemia
entities.subtitle: Hereditary King of Bohemia
entities.body: The hereditary King of Bohemia, of the House of Ormstein. He is the masked visitor who called himself Count Von Kramm, and he has just torn off his mask and admitted who he is.

aliasRules.why: Holmes first says ‘your Majesty’ at 54, the deduction that unmasks the visitor; bind only from 55 (the King’s own admission) so the masked figure is never tied to the King before the reveal paragraph ends.
As above; capitalised variant (O 56, 61, 77, 83, 103, 252; M 77, 83, 103).
Holmes refers to the King.
Modern edition capitalises the same reference.

exclude.why: ‘the King of Scandinavia’ — Clotilde’s father, not the King of Bohemia.
Reveal paragraph (Holmes’s deduction); gated — not bound.

snapshots.body: Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, the thirty-year-old hereditary King of Bohemia, in London incognito. He is about to announce his betrothal to Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen and wants Holmes to recover a compromising photograph of himself with Irene Adler, which she has threatened to send to his bride’s family.
snapshots.why: 56 (full name), 59–102 (the affair, the photograph, the betrothal and Irene’s threat).

snapshots.body: Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, hereditary King of Bohemia. Irene Adler’s letter convinces him she will never use the photograph, and he declares himself satisfied. He gives Holmes her portrait as a reward; Holmes takes it, bows, and turns away without taking the King’s outstretched hand.
snapshots.why: 247–257: outcome of the case.

entities.notes: He first appears masked under the alias Count Von Kramm (separate entity). Pre-reveal descriptions — ‘a gentleman’ in the note (21), ‘our strange visitor’ (49), ‘the august person who employs me’ (49), ‘his gigantic client’ (53), ‘The man’ (55) — are left unbound. Para 54 ‘your Majesty’ is the reveal and is excluded. ‘the King’ in 96 is the King of Scandinavia and is excluded. In 215 and 247 ‘the King of Bohemia’ resolves to the longer ‘King of Bohemia’. In 56 the full name and ‘King of Bohemia’ are two separate spans, both this entity.

entities.name: Count Von Kramm
entities.subtitle: Name given by a masked Bohemian visitor
entities.body: The name given to Holmes by a masked, very tall visitor with a strong German accent, who says he is a Bohemian nobleman.

aliasRules.why: ‘The Count shrugged’ (O) / ‘The Count’s broad shoulders’ (M): the masked visitor, before the reveal.

snapshots.name: Count Von Kramm (the King of Bohemia)
snapshots.body: A false name. The masked visitor who called himself Count Von Kramm, a Bohemian nobleman, is the King of Bohemia himself. He tears off his mask after Holmes addresses him as ‘your Majesty’.
snapshots.why: 49: he admits the title is not his own; 54: Holmes says ‘your Majesty’; 55: ‘I am the King.’

entities.notes: Disguise/alias entity. Must never be bound to king-of-bohemia before the end of 55. At 104 (‘You will find me at the Langham under the name of the Count Von Kramm’) the alias is post-reveal and shows the snapshot.

entities.name: Slim youth in an ulster
entities.subtitle: Passer-by who greets Holmes in Baker Street
entities.body: A slim young man in an ulster who hurries past Holmes’s door in Baker Street at night and wishes him good night by name. Holmes is sure he has heard the voice before.

aliasRules.why: The figure as described in the original.

aliasRules.alias: slender young man in an ulster
aliasRules.why: Modern rendering of the same phrase.

snapshots.name: Slim youth in an ulster (Irene Adler)
snapshots.body: Irene Adler in men’s clothes. After the fire alarm she suspected the clergyman, put on what she calls her ‘walking clothes’, followed Holmes home to make sure who he was, and then wished him good night.
snapshots.why: 242: she changed into male costume and came down as he left; 243: ‘I followed you to your door… Then I… wished you good-night.’

entities.notes: Concealed identity. ‘ulster’ also occurs at 192 (Watson’s own ulster) — not bound. Do not bind ‘youth’/‘young man’ globally.

entities.name: Godfrey Norton
entities.subtitle: Lawyer of the Inner Temple
entities.body: A dark, handsome lawyer of the Inner Temple and Irene Adler’s only regular male visitor, who calls at Briony Lodge once or twice a day.

aliasRules.why: ‘saved the bridegroom’ — Godfrey Norton, named earlier in the same paragraph.
After the wedding (141): Holmes’s argument (232) and the servant’s report (237).
Irene’s letter: ‘started for the Temple to see my husband’.

snapshots.body: A dark, handsome lawyer of the Inner Temple who has just married Irene Adler in a hurried ceremony at the Church of St. Monica, with the disguised Holmes dragged in as their witness.
snapshots.why: 141: the wedding.

snapshots.body: A lawyer of the Inner Temple and Irene Adler’s new husband. The morning after the wedding the couple leave England for the Continent on the 5:15 train from Charing Cross.
snapshots.why: 237: the servant reports their departure.

entities.notes: Holmes initially wonders whether Irene is his client, friend or mistress (130); the card avoids guessing. 228 ‘an English lawyer named Norton’ bound via ‘Norton’. Uppercase ‘NORTON’ in 246 belongs to Irene’s signature (‘IRENE NORTON’), not to him.

entities.name: Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen
entities.subtitle: Second daughter of the King of Scandinavia
entities.body: The second daughter of the King of Scandinavia, from a family of strict principles, whom the King of Bohemia is about to marry.

aliasRules.why: ‘his princess’ — Holmes refers to the King’s intended bride.

entities.notes: Mentioned only; never appears. Her father, ‘the King of Scandinavia’ (96), is left unbound.

entities.name: John
entities.subtitle: Irene Adler’s coachman
entities.body: The coachman who drives Irene Adler’s landau.

aliasRules.why: 134: the landau’s coachman (she calls him John in 135); 206: ‘the coachman had come in’ at Briony Lodge; 242: ‘John, the coachman’.
Only these two paragraphs; ‘John’ also occurs in ‘St. John’s Wood’ (116) and ‘Mr. John Hare’ (170).

exclude.why: The actor John Hare (bound to john-hare).

entities.notes: Not Watson (Watson is never called John in this story). In 242 Irene says she sent John to watch Holmes; card stays neutral.

entities.name: Mrs. Turner
entities.subtitle: Landlady at Baker Street in this story
entities.body: The landlady at the Baker Street lodgings, who brings Holmes a tray of supper.

aliasRules.why: 120: ‘The landlady’/‘His landlady’ tells Watson when Holmes went out; 155: ‘our landlady’, explicitly the Mrs. Turner of the same sentence.

entities.notes: NOT Mrs. Hudson; Mrs. Hudson does not appear in this story. 120’s landlady is unnamed but is the Baker Street landlady on the same afternoon as 155.

entities.name: Elderly servant at Briony Lodge
entities.subtitle: Servant at Briony Lodge
entities.body: An elderly woman on the steps of Briony Lodge who watches Holmes’s party with a sardonic eye and greets him by name.

aliasRules.why: Her introduction.
‘He pushed past the servant’ / ‘brushed past the servant’.

entities.notes: Speaks at 235, 237, 239. ‘servant’ elsewhere (8 ‘servant girl’, 193 ‘servant maids’) is not her and is outside the rule.

entities.name: Clergyman at St. Monica’s
entities.subtitle: Clergyman at the Church of St. Monica
entities.body: The clergyman in a surplice at the Church of St. Monica in the Edgeware Road, seen arguing with a couple at the altar.

aliasRules.why: Introduction.
Introduction (modern rendering).
Both occurrences in 141 are the officiating clergyman.

exclude.why: Holmes’s Nonconformist-clergyman disguise — Holmes, not this man.
Irene’s ‘dear, kind old clergyman’ is Holmes in disguise.

entities.notes: Not to be confused with Holmes’s clergyman disguise (170, 242).

entities.name: Mary Jane
entities.subtitle: Watson’s servant girl
entities.body: The clumsy, careless servant girl in Watson’s household, whom his wife has given notice.

aliasRules.why: Holmes’s deduction about Watson’s ‘servant girl’, named Mary Jane in 9.

entities.notes: Mentioned only. Watson’s wife (‘my wife’, 9) is unnamed here and left unbound.

entities.name: John Hare
entities.subtitle: English stage actor
entities.body: An English actor of Watson’s day, named as the only performer who could have equalled Holmes in a part.
entities.notes: Text has ‘Mr. John Hare’ (170, both editions); bind ‘John Hare’. Including him also prevents ‘John’ here from being read as the coachman.

entities.name: Jabez Wilson
entities.subtitle: Red-headed pawnbroker and Holmes’s client
entities.body: A stout, elderly pawnbroker with blazing red hair who runs a small business in Saxe-Coburg Square, near the City. He has come to Holmes with a strange story about a newspaper advertisement.

aliasRules.why: Narration describing the client Holmes has just introduced as Mr. Wilson.
The client of paragraph 11, unambiguously Wilson.
Modern wording of the same phrase.
Watson inspecting Wilson.
Watson inspecting Wilson.
Wilson pausing in his narrative.
Wilson reacting to the laughter.
Wilson has just left Baker Street.
Wilson’s shop sign in Saxe-Coburg Square.

snapshots.body: A stout, elderly red-headed pawnbroker from Saxe-Coburg Square. Hired by the Red-Headed League to copy the Encyclopædia Britannica for £4 a week, he worked eight weeks until he found the office locked and a card announcing that the League was dissolved.
snapshots.why: 88–92: his account of the job and the dissolution notice.

entities.notes: Name-alias spans: 22 per edition (21 ‘Wilson’ incl. compounds + ‘JABEZ WILSON’ shop sign at 137); +7 listed generic phrases per edition. At 141 ‘Mr. Wilson’s assistant’ binds only ‘Mr. Wilson’ (the assistant phrase is left unbound to avoid overlapping spans). At 5 ‘This gentleman’ means Watson, not Wilson. At 178 ‘the good pawnbroker’ (O) / ‘our good pawnbroker’ (M) and 208 ‘our friend’s premises’ also mean Wilson but are left unbound (low value).

entities.name: Vincent Spaulding
entities.subtitle: Jabez Wilson’s pawnshop assistant
entities.body: Jabez Wilson’s assistant at the pawnshop. Wilson says he is very capable and could earn twice as much elsewhere, but works for half wages to learn the business.

aliasRules.why: Holmes to Wilson, about Spaulding.
Holmes to Wilson, about Spaulding (capitalised in modern-en).
Wilson speaking of Spaulding.
The young man who opens Wilson’s door; 141 identifies him as Mr. Wilson’s assistant.
Holmes’s explanation, released with the 205 reveal.
Holmes’s explanation.
Modern wording.

snapshots.body: Jabez Wilson’s assistant, who works for half wages to learn the business. He showed Wilson the Red-Headed League’s advertisement, urged him to apply, and pushed him through the crowd of applicants. Wilson’s only complaint is his passion for photography, which keeps him in the cellar developing pictures.
snapshots.why: 37 (photography/cellar), 40–56 (he brings the advertisement and takes Wilson to apply).

snapshots.body: Jabez Wilson’s assistant: a small, quick, beardless man of about thirty with an acid stain on his forehead and pierced ears. He showed Wilson the League’s advertisement and pushed him to apply. After a brief look at him, Holmes calls him the fourth smartest man in London and says he has known something of him before.
snapshots.why: 121–123 description; 137–140 Holmes’s visit and remarks.

snapshots.name: Vincent Spaulding (John Clay)
snapshots.body: The name John Clay used while working as Jabez Wilson’s assistant. Holmes explains that he took the job at half wages, urged Wilson to apply to the sham League, and used the hours Wilson was away to dig a tunnel from the cellar to the bank behind the shop.
snapshots.why: 205 makes the assistant the second rogue in Clay’s scheme (one rogue kept the office, the other urged Wilson to apply); 207–208 confirm the cellar tunnel.

entities.notes: 8 name spans per edition + 10 listed generic phrases. Kept separate from john-clay: never bind ‘Spaulding’ or ‘the assistant’ to john-clay, and never mention Clay in any card released before the end of 205. At 34 ‘this obliging youth’ and 161 ‘this smooth-faced pawnbroker’s assistant’ (O) / ‘the clean-shaven pawnbroker’s assistant’ (M) are left unbound; 141 ‘Mr. Wilson’s assistant’ left unbound because ‘Mr. Wilson’ is bound to jabez-wilson.

entities.name: John Clay
entities.subtitle: Notorious young criminal
entities.body: A young master criminal—murderer, thief, passer of counterfeit coin and forger—whom Peter Jones of Scotland Yard names as the man he most wants to arrest. Jones says Clay has royal ancestry, went to Eton and Oxford, and has never been seen by him despite years of pursuit.

aliasRules.why: Clay as he is handcuffed; already named at 194.

snapshots.body: A notorious young criminal whom Peter Jones of Scotland Yard has hunted for years. Holmes names him as the clean-cut, boyish young man who climbs up through the floor of the bank cellar.
snapshots.why: 194: Holmes addresses the intruder as John Clay.

snapshots.body: A notorious young criminal whom Peter Jones of Scotland Yard has hunted for years. Caught climbing up through the floor of the bank cellar, he is handcuffed by Jones, insists on his royal blood, and is led off coolly to the police station.
snapshots.why: 199–202: arrest and removal in custody.

snapshots.body: A notorious young criminal caught tunnelling into the bank cellar and arrested by Peter Jones. Holmes explains that Clay, under the name Vincent Spaulding, had worked as Jabez Wilson’s assistant and devised the Red-Headed League with a red-haired accomplice to get Wilson out of the shop each day.
snapshots.why: 205: Holmes’s account makes Clay the assistant who urged Wilson to apply.

entities.notes: 7 name spans per edition (O 170 ‘Mr. John Clay’, M 170 ‘Mr. Clay’) + ‘our prisoner’ at 200. ‘the intruder’ at 193 and ‘a clean-cut, boyish face’ at 191 are deliberately unbound: he is not named until 194. ‘the man upon whom you wish to lay your hands’ (168) unbound.

entities.name: Duncan Ross
entities.subtitle: Manager of the Red-Headed League’s office
entities.body: The man named in the Red-Headed League’s newspaper advertisement as the person to apply to at the League’s offices, 7 Pope’s Court, Fleet Street.

aliasRules.why: Wilson’s word for the small red-headed man who interviews him and introduces himself as Duncan Ross at 62.

snapshots.body: A small man with hair even redder than Jabez Wilson’s, who interviews the applicants at 7 Pope’s Court, chooses Wilson, and says he is himself a pensioner of the League’s fund.
snapshots.why: 58–62: interview and self-introduction.

snapshots.body: The red-headed man who hired Jabez Wilson for the Red-Headed League. After the League closed, the landlord said he had never heard the name: he knew the tenant as William Morris, a solicitor, and the forwarding address turned out to be a factory where nobody knew either name.
snapshots.why: 96–103: landlord’s account and the false forwarding address.

snapshots.body: The man who ran the Red-Headed League’s office and hired Jabez Wilson. Holmes explains that the League was a scheme by John Clay and his red-haired accomplice to keep Wilson away from his shop: one rogue kept the temporary office while the other urged Wilson to apply.
snapshots.why: 205: Holmes’s explanation identifies the office-keeper as Clay’s red-haired accomplice.

entities.notes: 7 name spans per edition (O 87 ‘Mr. Duncan Ross’, M 87 ‘Mr. Ross’) + ‘the manager’ at 61 and 87. ‘a small man’ / ‘the little man’ (58, O only) and ‘the other’ (60) left unbound. The text never states outright that Duncan Ross is the red-haired companion Clay calls Archie (192); it is implied by 205. Do not bind Archie or William Morris to this entity.

entities.name: William Morris
entities.subtitle: Name the Pope’s Court landlord gives for the League office’s tenant
entities.body: The name the landlord at 7 Pope’s Court gives for the red-headed man who rented the room used as the League’s office—the man Jabez Wilson knew as Duncan Ross. The landlord says he was a solicitor who moved out the day before.

snapshots.body: The name the landlord at 7 Pope’s Court gives for the red-headed tenant Jabez Wilson knew as Duncan Ross. The forwarding address, 17 King Edward Street, proved to be an artificial-kneecap factory where no one had heard of either name.
snapshots.why: 102–103: false forwarding address.

entities.notes: A second name for the same tenant; kept as its own entity per the alias rule, since the true owner of either name is not settled. The Morris = Ross link is made in the same paragraph as the first mention (97–100). No thread entry: it first appears mid-story.

entities.name: Archie
entities.subtitle: Red-haired man in the bank cellar
entities.body: A small, pale young man with a shock of very red hair who is pulled up through the cellar floor by the first intruder. His companion calls him Archie.

snapshots.body: The small, pale, red-haired man who came up through the cellar floor with John Clay and dived back down the hole when Holmes sprang. Holmes says three men were waiting at the house’s door, and that Clay took the idea for the Red-Headed League from the colour of his accomplice’s hair.
snapshots.why: 193–199 escape; 196 men at the door; 205 Holmes’s account of Clay’s red-haired accomplice.

entities.notes: Only the name ‘Archie’ is bound. ‘a companion’ (191), ‘The other’ (193), ‘my pal’ (O 195) / ‘my friend’ (M 195), ‘your pal’ (O 199) / ‘your friend’ (M 199) left unbound. His capture is not shown (Jones only predicts it at 199). The text implies but never states that he is the man who called himself Duncan Ross; the snapshot quotes Holmes rather than asserting the link. No thread entry: any start-of-story description would anticipate the climax.

entities.name: Peter Jones
entities.subtitle: Scotland Yard police agent
entities.body: Peter Jones, an official police agent from Scotland Yard whom Watson already knows. He is waiting with Holmes at Baker Street for the night’s expedition.

aliasRules.why: Jones speaking to Merryweather.
Jones leading Clay away.

snapshots.body: Peter Jones of Scotland Yard, self-important but, Holmes says, as brave as a bulldog and as tenacious as a lobster. In the bank cellar he handcuffs John Clay and takes him to the police station.
snapshots.why: 172 Holmes’s assessment; 199–202 arrest.

entities.notes: Not Athelney Jones by name: ‘Athelney’ does not occur. His mention of ‘the Sholto murder and the Agra treasure’ (166) refers to another case; do not import details. M 166 ‘the policeman’ left unbound (generic). Card avoids the rank ‘inspector’ because this story does not give him one.

entities.name: Mr. Merryweather
entities.subtitle: Sad-faced, respectable gentleman on Holmes’s night expedition
entities.body: A long, thin, sad-faced man with a shiny hat and an oppressively respectable frock-coat, introduced by Holmes as a companion for the night’s adventure.

aliasRules.why: Merryweather replying to Jones; M 131 ‘the stranger’ is a comparative adjective and is not covered.
Merryweather explaining the French gold.
Watson distinguishing Merryweather’s breathing from Jones’s.

snapshots.body: A long, thin, sad-faced man with a shiny hat and an oppressively respectable frock-coat, introduced by Holmes as a companion for the night’s adventure. He laments missing his Saturday-night game of cards for the first time in twenty-seven years.
snapshots.why: Raised at 2:167.

snapshots.body: A long, thin, sad-faced man in an oppressively respectable frock-coat. Holmes explains that he is a bank director with a personal interest in the night’s business.
snapshots.why: 172: Holmes names him a bank director.

snapshots.body: Chairman of the directors of one of the principal London banks. He leads the party into the cellar of its City branch, where the bank keeps 30,000 French napoleons borrowed from the Bank of France and has had warnings of an attempt on them.
snapshots.why: 178–181: the bank, the cellar and the French gold.

entities.notes: Subtitle deliberately avoids ‘bank director’: that is revealed at 172, and his link to the bank anticipates the target of the plot. No first name given.

entities.name: Ezekiah Hopkins
entities.subtitle: Benefactor named in the Red-Headed League’s advertisement
entities.body: The late benefactor of Lebanon, Pennsylvania, named in the Red-Headed League’s advertisement; the notice says his bequest funds a vacancy paying £4 a week for nominal work.

snapshots.body: The late benefactor named in the Red-Headed League’s advertisement. According to Vincent Spaulding, he was an eccentric American millionaire, red-headed himself, who left his fortune in trust to provide easy, well-paid posts for red-headed men.
snapshots.why: 52: Spaulding’s account of the founder.

entities.notes: Only mentioned. The text never explicitly says he did not exist; cards attribute everything to the advertisement and Spaulding. Holmes’s 205 explanation exposes the League as a ruse, but no snapshot asserts Hopkins was invented.

entities.name: Sarasate
entities.subtitle: Spanish violinist (1844–1908)
entities.body: Pablo de Sarasate, the celebrated Spanish violin virtuoso and composer. Holmes invites Watson to hear him play at St. James’s Hall.
entities.notes: Real historical person.

entities.name: Gustave Flaubert
entities.subtitle: French novelist (1821–1880)
entities.body: French novelist, author of Madame Bovary. Holmes quotes a line he attributes to Flaubert’s letters to George Sand: ‘The man is nothing; the work is everything.’
entities.notes: Real historical person; quotation attributed by Holmes.

entities.name: George Sand
entities.subtitle: French novelist (1804–1876)
entities.body: Pen name of the French novelist Aurore Dupin, a friend and long-time correspondent of Gustave Flaubert.
entities.notes: Real historical person.

entities.name: Mary Sutherland
entities.subtitle: Holmes’s client; a typist from Camberwell
entities.body: A client of Holmes’s whose “very simple problem” he mentions in passing. Her own case is told in A Case of Identity.

aliasRules.why: Watson’s description of Mary as she leaves; unambiguous and not spoiling. Elsewhere ‘our visitor’ is Windibank.

snapshots.body: A short-sighted young typist with a small private income of her own. She has come to Holmes in distress to find out what has become of her fiancé, Mr. Hosmer Angel.
snapshots.why: Her own story opens; the reviewed setup identity applies from her first paragraph in story 3.

snapshots.body: A short-sighted young typist with a small private income. Her vanished fiancé ‘Hosmer Angel’ was her stepfather in disguise, but Holmes decides not to tell her, believing she would not accept it. She has vowed to stay true to Hosmer.
snapshots.why: Holmes’s decision at 3:136.

entities.notes: Before her name at 13 she is described at 11–12 as ‘a large woman’ / ‘the maiden’ (O) / ‘the young lady’ (M 12); left unbound. Generic ‘the young lady’, ‘the girl’, ‘the daughter’, ‘the maiden’ (81) left unbound. Counts: 8 name spans plus ‘our visitor’ at 79 in each edition. Her address (No. 31 Lyon Place, Camberwell) is at 74; subtitle draws on 13–15 and 74.

entities.name: Hosmer Angel
entities.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s vanished fiancé
entities.body: The man Mary Sutherland was engaged to. He has disappeared, and she has come to Holmes to find out what became of him.

snapshots.body: A shy, softly spoken gentleman, as Mary describes him, whom she met at the gasfitters’ ball and became engaged to. On their wedding morning he got into a separate cab to the church and was not in it when it arrived.
snapshots.why: Wedding-morning disappearance told at 3:56.

snapshots.name: Hosmer Angel (false identity)
snapshots.body: Not a real man. Holmes shows that ‘Hosmer Angel’ was Mary’s stepfather, James Windibank, in disguise, with tinted glasses, false whiskers and a whispering voice. He used it, with his wife’s help, to court Mary himself and so keep her and her income at home.
snapshots.why: 124 is where Holmes states outright that the stepfather disguised himself and ‘appears as Mr. Hosmer Angel’ (both editions). The hints at 118–122 (‘I have caught him!’, Windibank’s panic) are not an explicit identification, so the gate is the end of 124.

entities.notes: Must stay a separate entity from james-windibank. Do not merge or link the cards before the end of [3,124]. Includes the typed signature ‘Hosmer Angel’ at 94 and the advertisement at 91. 40 has ‘Hosmer—Mr. Angel’ as two spans of the same entity. Counts: 23 spans containing ‘Hosmer’ plus 4 standalone ‘Mr. Angel’ (40, 75, 92, 126) per edition. Pronouns and ‘the gentleman’ / ‘the missing man’ / ‘the disappearing bridegroom’ (100) are unbound. Kind is kept as ‘person’ so that the kind label gives nothing away.

entities.name: Mr. Windibank
entities.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s stepfather
entities.body: Mary Sutherland’s stepfather, only about five years older than she is. He married her widowed mother and works as a travelling salesman for a wine importer. He refused to go to the police or to Holmes about her missing fiancé.

aliasRules.why: In these paragraphs ‘father’ is Mary’s name for her stepfather (or Holmes’s ‘your father’). In 23 and 30 ‘father’ is her late father, so those are excluded by omission.
Same referent as above, lower-case in modern.
Modern capitalises Mary’s ‘Father’ for the stepfather here. ‘Father’ in M 23 and M 30 is her late father.
Always Windibank in this story. Binding in 124–132 is at or after the reveal.
Watson’s narration for Windibank while he is in the room; not spoiling.
Sentence-initial form, both editions.
O 127 is sentence-initial; M 127 uses lower-case (covered above).

exclude.why: Mary’s late father, the plumber (late-mr-sutherland); not covered by the paragraph rules.
‘send father tickets when he was alive’ / ‘father’s friends’ means the late father (late-mr-sutherland).

snapshots.name: James Windibank
snapshots.body: Mary Sutherland’s stepfather. Holmes shows that, with his wife’s help, he disguised himself as ‘Hosmer Angel’ and courted Mary so that she, and the hundred a year he had the use of, would stay at home.
snapshots.why: 124: Holmes’s account explicitly identifies the stepfather as the man who ‘appears as Mr. Hosmer Angel’.

snapshots.name: James Windibank
snapshots.body: Mary Sutherland’s stepfather, who disguised himself as ‘Hosmer Angel’ to keep her and her income at home. Faced with the evidence, he claimed it began as a joke and insisted that nothing he did was legally actionable. He fled when Holmes reached for a hunting crop.
snapshots.why: 125–129: his response to the accusation and his flight.

entities.notes: First name James is given only from 108; the first display name is ‘Mr. Windibank’. Counts: name spans O 20 / M 21 (M 134 adds ‘Windibank’ where O says ‘the man himself’). Rule spans: father/Father O 13 / M 12, stepfather 9 / 9, our visitor 4 / 4. ‘The man’ at 123 and pronouns are left unbound. He is NOT Watson; Watson is never called James or John in this story. The typed letter at 110 and the typewriter evidence (114–116) are attributed to him by Holmes, but the Hosmer link is gated to the end of 124.

entities.name: Mary Sutherland’s mother
entities.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s mother
entities.body: Mary’s mother, a plumber’s widow who has remarried. Her new husband, Mr. Windibank, is nearly fifteen years younger than she is. She lives with him and Mary in Camberwell.

aliasRules.why: Mary’s or Holmes’s references to her mother, unambiguous in each listed paragraph.
Lower-case occurrences in modern.
Sentence-initial ‘Mother said…’, ‘Mother was all in his favour…’
Modern capitalises Mary’s ‘Mother’.
‘connivance and assistance of his wife’ / ‘his wife’s knowledge’ refers to her. In 3–4 ‘his wife’ belongs to newspaper/Dundas cases and stays unbound.

snapshots.body: Mary’s mother, who remarried the much younger James Windibank. Holmes concludes that she knew of and helped with her husband’s disguise as ‘Hosmer Angel’, which explains her enthusiasm for the suitor.
snapshots.why: 124: ‘With the connivance and assistance of his wife’; Windibank’s ‘We never thought…’ at 125 confirms it.

entities.notes: Never named in the text; ‘Mrs. Windibank’ does not occur, so don’t invent it. Her fondness for Hosmer (52) and her anger and ban on discussing the matter (64) are clues, so the first card stays neutral. Counts: O mother 10 + Mother 2 + his wife 1; M mother 3 + Mother 8 + his wife 1.

entities.name: Mary Sutherland’s late father
entities.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s late father, a plumber
entities.body: Mary’s father, now dead. He ran a plumbing business in the Tottenham Court Road, which her mother carried on for a time before selling it.

aliasRules.why: 23: ‘father’s death’, ‘father could have got’; 30: ‘send father tickets when he was alive’, ‘father’s friends’.
‘Father was a plumber…’
Modern capitalises all late-father references in 23 and 30.

entities.notes: Unnamed. His surname is only implied as Sutherland (Holmes infers ‘stepfather’ because ‘the name is different’, 20), so the display name avoids asserting it. The namesake trap is ‘father’, which elsewhere means Windibank.

entities.name: Mr. Hardy
entities.subtitle: Former foreman of the Sutherland family’s plumbing business
entities.body: The foreman of the plumbing business left by Mary’s late father. He escorted Mary and her mother to the gasfitters’ ball.
entities.notes: Occurs at 23 and 30. The body draws on 30 (the ball escort), which is ordinary setup.

entities.name: Uncle Ned
entities.subtitle: Mary Sutherland’s uncle in Auckland
entities.body: Mary’s uncle in Auckland, New Zealand. He left her £2,500 in New Zealand stock, and she receives only the interest from it.
entities.notes: The text says the money ‘was left me by my uncle Ned’, which implies he has died; the subtitle’s ‘late’ rests on that. His legacy is the motive for the plot, but saying he provided her income is not a spoiler.

entities.name: Mrs. Etherege
entities.subtitle: Recommended Holmes to Mary Sutherland
entities.body: An acquaintance of Mary’s whose husband Holmes found after the police had given him up for dead. She told Mary about Holmes.
entities.notes: Her husband (‘whose husband you found’) is left unbound.

entities.name: Westhouse & Marbank
entities.subtitle: Claret importers of Fenchurch Street
entities.body: A large firm of claret importers in Fenchurch Street. Mr. Windibank travels for them.

snapshots.body: The claret importers of Fenchurch Street who employ James Windibank as a traveller. When Holmes sent them the Hosmer Angel description with the disguise removed, they replied that it matched Windibank in every respect.
snapshots.why: 134 reveals that the ‘firm in the City’ of 98 was this one, and that it confirmed the identification.

entities.notes: ‘a firm in the City’ (98) is left unbound until it is named at 134, so that Holmes’s inquiry is not exposed early. Drop this entry if firms are out of scope.

entities.name: Balzac
entities.subtitle: French novelist (1799–1850)
entities.body: Honoré de Balzac, the French novelist. Holmes notes that Hosmer Angel’s letters quote him once.
entities.notes: Real person; the identification is standard general knowledge.

entities.name: Hafiz
entities.subtitle: Fourteenth-century Persian poet
entities.body: The Persian poet Hafiz. Holmes cites ‘the old Persian saying’ and puts his wisdom on a level with Horace’s.
entities.notes: Final paragraph only.

entities.name: Horace
entities.subtitle: Roman poet (65–8 BC)
entities.body: The Latin poet Horace, whom Holmes pairs with Hafiz as a source of worldly wisdom.
entities.notes: Final paragraph only.

entities.name: John Turner
entities.subtitle: Boscombe Valley landowner
entities.body: The largest landowner in Boscombe Valley, who made his fortune in Australia and came home to England some years ago. A widower with one daughter, he knew Charles McCarthy in the colonies and lets him Hatherley Farm.

aliasRules.why: ‘The old man’/‘the old man’ is Turner, the announced visitor, in these paragraphs only; binding after 185 names nobody new and the guilt gate is carried by snapshots, not by this binding.
McCarthy addresses Turner as ‘Jack’ in Turner’s own confession, after the Black Jack alias is revealed at 202.

snapshots.body: The largest landowner in Boscombe Valley, about sixty, who made his fortune in the Victorian goldfields. Long in poor health, he has taken to his bed since McCarthy’s death. Lestrade says he was McCarthy’s great benefactor and let him have Hatherley Farm rent free.
snapshots.why: Lestrade’s information at 4:119.

snapshots.body: The largest landowner in Boscombe Valley, an old acquaintance of Charles McCarthy from the Australian colonies and his landlord. Gravely ill, he comes to Holmes at the hotel; when Holmes says he knows all about McCarthy, Turner breaks down and says he would have spoken out rather than let young McCarthy be condemned.
snapshots.why: Paragraphs 191–192: Holmes confronts him and Turner effectively admits responsibility for McCarthy’s death. First point the reader learns the culprit.

snapshots.body: The largest landowner in Boscombe Valley, dying of diabetes. In a signed confession he tells Holmes that he was once the goldfields bushranger Black Jack of Ballarat; that Charles McCarthy, the convoy driver whose life he spared, later found him in England and blackmailed him for twenty years; and that he struck McCarthy down at Boscombe Pool when McCarthy pressed for James to marry his daughter Alice.
snapshots.why: Paragraphs 202–208 give the full confession: alias, blackmail, motive and the killing.

snapshots.body: The largest landowner in Boscombe Valley. He confessed to Holmes that he, once the bushranger Black Jack of Ballarat, killed his blackmailer Charles McCarthy at Boscombe Pool. Holmes kept the confession unused, and Turner lived seven months more before he died. Watson writes that his daughter and young McCarthy may yet live happily together, unaware of the past.
snapshots.why: Paragraph 214 reports his death seven months later.

entities.notes: Every bare ‘Turner’ in this story is John Turner (including ‘Turner’s daughter’ at 16/122); his daughter always appears as ‘Miss Turner’ (longer match) or ‘Alice’. Do NOT bind ‘the murderer’, ‘the culprit’, ‘the criminal’, ‘the gentleman I describe’ or Holmes’s description at 143 to him. 185 announces him by name right after Watson’s ‘The culprit is—’ (184); this is a dramatic cut, not a reveal, so no snapshot fires before 192. ‘My doctor’ (198) is probably Dr. Willows but is left unbound. O 214 ‘Old Turner’ is capitalised (M just ‘Turner’).

entities.name: Charles McCarthy
entities.subtitle: Tenant of Hatherley Farm
entities.body: A former Australian colonist who rents Hatherley Farm from his old acquaintance John Turner. A widower with one son, James.

exclude.why: ‘if McCarthy is condemned/convicted’ means James McCarthy (bound to james-mccarthy by rule).

snapshots.body: A former Australian colonist who rented Hatherley Farm from his old acquaintance John Turner, a widower with one son, James. On Monday 3 June he walked to Boscombe Pool for an important three o’clock appointment and never came back alive.
snapshots.why: Paragraph 17: ‘From that appointment he never came back alive.’

snapshots.body: A former Australian colonist who rented Hatherley Farm from his old acquaintance John Turner, a widower with one son, James. On Monday 3 June he walked to Boscombe Pool for an important three o’clock appointment and never came back alive. His son describes him as cold and forbidding in manner and not a popular man.
snapshots.why: Manner described by 4:37.

snapshots.body: A former Australian colonist who lived rent-free at Hatherley Farm. John Turner’s confession reveals that McCarthy was the wagon-driver of a gold convoy that Turner’s gang robbed in Victoria; years later he recognised Turner in London and blackmailed him for twenty years. When he pressed for his son James to marry Turner’s daughter Alice, Turner killed him at Boscombe Pool.
snapshots.why: Paragraphs 203–208: wagon-driver, blackmail, the marriage demand and the killing.

entities.notes: Bare ‘McCarthy’ = Charles everywhere except 211 (excluded → James). James is caught by longer forms: ‘James McCarthy’, ‘young McCarthy’, ‘Young McCarthy’ (O 197, M 134), ‘young Mr. McCarthy’ (O 19), ‘McCarthy junior’ (O 127), ‘younger McCarthy’ (M 127). ‘Mr. McCarthy’ is always the father (18 O ×2, 19 O ×2, 84, 86, 90). M 127 ‘the elder’ and O 19 ‘Mr. McCarthy the elder’ (bound via ‘Mr. McCarthy’) refer to him. Plural ‘McCarthys’ is left unbound.

entities.name: James McCarthy
entities.subtitle: Charles McCarthy’s son
entities.body: The eighteen-year-old only son of Charles McCarthy of Hatherley Farm. Like his father, he is fond of sport and often seen at local race meetings.

aliasRules.why: Holmes’s ‘if McCarthy is condemned’ (M ‘convicted’) refers to the accused son.

snapshots.body: The eighteen-year-old only son of Charles McCarthy. He reported finding his father dying beside Boscombe Pool; a witness had seen the two quarrelling, his gun lay near the body and there was blood on his hand. The police arrested him, the inquest returned a verdict of wilful murder, and he awaits trial at the Assizes.
snapshots.why: Paragraph 19: arrest, inquest verdict and committal to the Assizes.

snapshots.body: The eighteen-year-old son of Charles McCarthy, held for trial for his father’s murder; Miss Turner and Holmes believe him innocent. Holmes learns that he loves Miss Turner but, about two years ago, secretly married a Bristol barmaid. That is why he resisted his father’s pressure to propose, and why he spent the days before the killing in Bristol. The barmaid has now broken with him, revealing she already had a husband.
snapshots.why: Paragraph 113 reveals the secret marriage and its collapse.

snapshots.body: The son of Charles McCarthy, wrongly held for his father’s murder. He had secretly married a Bristol barmaid who turned out to be married already. He was acquitted at the Assizes on objections Holmes prepared for the defence, and may yet marry Alice Turner without ever learning the truth about the past.
snapshots.why: Paragraph 214: acquittal and hoped-for future.

entities.notes: Before 18 he is only ‘the son of the murdered man’ (13) and ‘one son’ (16) — generic, unbound. ‘Witness’ in the inquest transcript (39–65) is James but is left unbound (role label). All ‘James’ alone (76, 82, 84 ×2, 96) are Alice speaking of him.

entities.name: Miss Turner
entities.subtitle: John Turner’s daughter
entities.body: John Turner’s only daughter, about eighteen. She believes James McCarthy is innocent and has engaged Lestrade, and through him Holmes, on his behalf.

snapshots.name: Miss Turner
snapshots.body: John Turner’s only daughter, who has known James McCarthy since childhood and is sure he is innocent. She brought in Lestrade and Holmes to clear him. She tells Holmes that Charles McCarthy wanted her to marry James, a match both James and her father opposed.
snapshots.why: Her interview with Holmes ends at 4:86.

snapshots.name: Alice Turner
snapshots.body: Alice Turner, John Turner’s only daughter, who has known James McCarthy since childhood and is sure he is innocent. She brought in Lestrade and Holmes to clear him. She told Holmes that Charles McCarthy wanted her to marry James, a match her father opposed.
snapshots.why: Paragraph 200 gives her first name (Turner: ‘I should wish to spare Alice the shock’). No spoiler added.

entities.notes: ‘Alice Turner’ never appears as a string; the snapshot display name combines ‘Alice’ (200, 203, 206 ×2) with ‘Miss Turner’. At 16 ‘Turner had an only daughter’ binds ‘Turner’ to John; ‘daughter’, ‘my dear girl’, ‘my girl’ are unbound. She is the unnamed ‘lady’ at 74 (unbound).

entities.name: Lestrade
entities.subtitle: Scotland Yard detective
entities.body: A Scotland Yard detective whom Holmes and Watson know from an earlier case. A practical, sceptical man, he brings Holmes in when a case puzzles him.

aliasRules.why: ‘the detective’ (O) / ‘The detective’ (M) at 130 is Lestrade, walking behind Holmes with Watson.

entities.notes: SHARED id; introduced in this story, recurs in story 10. Body kept book-general (no Boscombe-specific detail). M 131 ‘turned to Lestrade’ renders O ‘turned upon my companion’, so M has one extra Lestrade. ‘my colleague’ at 81 is Lestrade speaking of Holmes (trap; unbound).

entities.name: William Crowder
entities.subtitle: Gamekeeper to John Turner
entities.body: A gamekeeper employed by John Turner. He testified that he saw Charles McCarthy walking towards Boscombe Pool, followed a few minutes later by his son carrying a gun.
entities.notes: O 18 says ‘The game-keeper adds’ where M says ‘Crowder adds’ (extra M occurrence). ‘the game-keeper’ generic left unbound.

entities.name: Patience Moran
entities.subtitle: Daughter of the Boscombe Valley lodge-keeper
entities.body: The fourteen-year-old daughter of the lodge-keeper on the Boscombe Valley estate. While picking flowers in the woods she saw Charles McCarthy and his son quarrelling violently by the pool.
entities.notes: ‘the little girl’ (31) is her but left unbound. Bare ‘Moran’ at 135 is NOT bound (see unbound).

entities.name: The lodge-keeper
entities.subtitle: Lodge-keeper of the Boscombe Valley estate
entities.body: The keeper of the lodge on John Turner’s Boscombe Valley estate and father of Patience Moran. His lodge was the nearest house to the pool.

aliasRules.why: Holmes goes into “the lodge” to have “a word with Moran”: the lodge-keeper, father of Patience Moran.

snapshots.body: Moran, keeper of the lodge on John Turner’s Boscombe Valley estate and father of Patience Moran. His lodge was the nearest house to the pool.
snapshots.why: Named at 4:135.
snapshots.name: Moran, the lodge-keeper

entities.notes: All five ‘lodge-keeper’ hits (19 ×2, 37, 134, 188) are the same man. He presumably shares the surname Moran (his daughter is Patience Moran; Holmes goes to the lodge to ‘have a word with Moran’ at 135), but the text never names him outright, so ‘Moran’ at 135 stays unbound.

entities.name: The coroner
entities.subtitle: Coroner at the McCarthy inquest
entities.body: The official who conducted the inquest into Charles McCarthy’s death and questioned James McCarthy closely about his story.
entities.notes: ‘The Coroner’ speaks in the transcript 38–54; lowercase ‘coroner’ 19, 27 (O ‘coroner’s jury’), 67, 68, 82 — all the same official. Category supporting (speaks) though minor.

entities.name: John Cobb
entities.subtitle: Groom at Hatherley Farm
entities.body: The McCarthys’ groom, who drove Charles McCarthy to Ross on the morning he died.
entities.notes: Mentioned once. The ‘serving-man’ (O 17) / ‘manservant’ (M 17) who went to Ross with McCarthy that morning is very probably Cobb, but the text does not equate them, so 17 is left unbound.

entities.name: Dr. Willows
entities.subtitle: John Turner’s doctor
entities.body: The doctor attending John Turner, who says Turner’s nerves are shattered and will not allow him visitors.

aliasRules.why: Alice’s ‘the doctor’ (O) / ‘his doctor’ (M) at 88–89 is named as Dr. Willows at 90; restricted to avoid Watson (a doctor) and the unattributed ‘My doctor’ at 198.

entities.notes: Name appears only at 90. Body uses only 88–90 facts.

entities.name: The Bristol barmaid
entities.subtitle: Barmaid in Bristol
entities.body: A barmaid in Bristol, mentioned by Holmes after his visit to James McCarthy in prison.

snapshots.body: A Bristol barmaid whom James McCarthy secretly married at a registry office about two years ago; he spent the three days before his father’s death with her. On reading that he might hang, she broke with him and wrote that she already had a husband in the Bermuda Dockyard.
snapshots.why: Paragraph 113 reveals the secret marriage, the Bristol alibi and her prior husband.

entities.notes: All three ‘barmaid’ hits per edition are in 113 (the reveal paragraph), so the first card must not mention the marriage. ‘his/this barmaid wife’ binds via ‘barmaid’. ‘she’/‘her’ unbound. Her husband in the Bermuda Dockyard is unbound.

entities.name: Black Jack of Ballarat
entities.subtitle: Bushranger name from the Victorian goldfields
entities.body: The name a highway robber went by on the Victorian goldfields in the early 1860s.

snapshots.name: Black Jack of Ballarat (John Turner)
snapshots.body: The name John Turner went under as a young highway robber on the Victorian goldfields in the early 1860s, one of the six men of the Ballarat Gang.
snapshots.why: Paragraph 202: Turner says ‘Black Jack of Ballarat was the name I went under’.

entities.notes: Alias entity per policy; mention and reveal fall in the same paragraph (202), so the first card names no owner. ‘Jack’ at 205 binds to john-turner (rule). Do not bind ‘so and so, of Ballarat’ / ‘an Australian from Ballarat’ (167, 169) to this or to Turner.

entities.name: The Ballarat Gang
entities.subtitle: Goldfields bushranger gang
entities.body: A band of six highway robbers on the Victorian goldfields in the early 1860s, still remembered in the colony.

snapshots.body: A band of six highway robbers on the Victorian goldfields in the early 1860s, still remembered in the colony. John Turner rode with them under the name Black Jack of Ballarat.
snapshots.why: Paragraph 202 places Turner in the gang.

entities.notes: Only one mention (202).

entities.name: Petrarch
entities.subtitle: Italian poet
entities.body: The fourteenth-century Italian poet. Holmes carries a pocket edition of his work to read on the train.
entities.notes: One mention.

entities.name: George Meredith
entities.subtitle: English novelist and poet
entities.body: A Victorian English novelist and poet, contemporary with the story. Holmes proposes discussing him to put the case aside for the evening.
entities.notes: One mention.

entities.name: John Openshaw
entities.subtitle: Young man from Horsham who consults Holmes
entities.body: A young man of about twenty-two who comes through a storm from Horsham, in Sussex, to ask Holmes for advice and help about a strange chain of events in his family.

aliasRules.why: Bare surname here clearly means John (Holmes’s ‘young Openshaw’, the newspaper name). Elsewhere bare ‘Openshaw’ means Elias or is ambiguous.
Holmes’s name for John.
Holmes’s name for John (modern drops ‘young’ at 125 and 135).
Holmes’s name for John.
Narration about John after he has named himself; 32 is left unbound because he is not yet named there.
Narration about the visitor; modern has ‘he’.
Holmes returns the diary page to John.

snapshots.body: The young man from Horsham who brought Holmes the story of the orange-pip warnings. A newspaper reports that his body was recovered from the Thames near Waterloo Bridge the same night he left Baker Street, and calls his death an accident.
snapshots.why: 146 is the newspaper account of his death.

snapshots.body: The young man from Horsham who brought Holmes the story of the orange-pip warnings, and who drowned near Waterloo Bridge that same night. Holmes traced the men he holds responsible to the barque Lone Star, and Watson’s narration calls them John Openshaw’s murderers; they were never brought to justice.
snapshots.why: 165–177: Holmes names the gang’s leader, plans a murder charge, and the narration calls the Lone Star men his murderers before the ship is lost.

entities.notes: Do NOT bind bare ‘Openshaw’ globally: 34 is the ‘Openshaw unbreakable tire/tyre’ (a product); 127 and 133 mean Elias; 163 (‘as Openshaw did before him’) is ambiguous between the three recipients of the pips and is left unbound. ‘John’ global is safe because ‘John Swain’ (88, 90) is its own longer alias. Not to be confused with Watson (who is never called John in this story).

entities.name: Elias Openshaw
entities.subtitle: John Openshaw’s uncle, a former colonel
entities.body: John Openshaw’s uncle. He emigrated to America as a young man, became a planter in Florida and a colonel in the Confederate army, then returned around 1869–70 to a small estate near Horsham, where he lived as a hard-drinking recluse.

aliasRules.why: John’s narration; means Elias. Not bound at 35 (‘rose to be a colonel’ is a rank, not a name).
Holmes means the man who carried the papers out of America, i.e. Elias.
John’s narration about Elias (34 is covered by ‘uncle Elias’).
John addressing Elias (‘What is it, uncle?’).
John’s narration about Elias (34 covered by ‘uncle Elias’).
John’s narration about Elias.
Modern uses capitalised ‘Uncle’ as a name for Elias (35 covered by ‘Uncle Elias’).
Holmes speaking to John about Elias.

snapshots.body: John Openshaw’s uncle, a former Confederate colonel who lived as a recluse near Horsham. Some weeks after a letter of five orange pips marked ‘K. K. K.’ arrived, he was found dead face-down in a shallow garden pool; the jury called it suicide, though John doubts it.
snapshots.why: 44 narrates his death and the suicide verdict.

snapshots.name: Colonel Elias Openshaw
snapshots.body: John Openshaw’s uncle, found dead in a shallow garden pool after receiving the orange-pip warning. Holmes believes he left America in 1869 carrying the papers of the Ku Klux Klan, and that several determined men, not chance, explain his death.
snapshots.why: 127 (Holmes: the deaths were the work of several men) and 133 (link between the Klan’s collapse and his flight with its papers).

entities.notes: O ‘my uncle’/M ‘Uncle’ differ by edition; rules are per edition. Holmes’s view that his death was murder is attributed, never asserted.

entities.name: Joseph Openshaw
entities.subtitle: John Openshaw’s father, Elias’s brother
entities.body: John Openshaw’s father and Elias Openshaw’s brother. He had a small factory at Coventry, patented the Openshaw unbreakable tyre for bicycles, and sold the business to retire comfortably.

aliasRules.why: John’s narration (34 is covered by ‘father Joseph’).
John’s narration.
John’s narration.
John’s narration.
Modern uses capitalised ‘Father’ as a name for Joseph.
Elias speaking to John about Joseph.

snapshots.body: John Openshaw’s father, who inherited the Horsham estate from his brother Elias. Days after receiving five orange pips and the order ‘Put the papers on the sundial’, he was found with a shattered skull in a chalk-pit near Portsdown Hill and died; the jury called it an accident, but John suspects a plot.
snapshots.why: 64 narrates his fall and death and the accident verdict.

entities.notes: ‘my brother’ in 42 (Elias’s will: ‘to my brother, your father’) is covered by ‘your father’. The inheritance (44) is in the snapshot, not the first card, since it depends on Elias’s death.

entities.name: K. K. K.
entities.subtitle: Initials on the orange-pip warnings
entities.body: Three letters, K. K. K., that Elias Openshaw sees on an envelope from Pondicherry holding five dried orange pips. He recognises them with terror, but what they stand for is not explained.

snapshots.body: Initials on the orange-pip warnings sent to the Openshaws. Holmes concludes they are not one person’s initials but the badge of a society: several resourceful men determined to recover papers Elias Openshaw took from America.
snapshots.why: 127: ‘K. K. K. ceases to be the initials of an individual and becomes the badge of a society.’

snapshots.name: Ku Klux Klan (K. K. K.)
snapshots.body: The Ku Klux Klan: a terrorist secret society formed by ex-Confederate soldiers after the American Civil War, which sent warnings such as orange pips before its murders. Holmes links its sudden collapse in 1869 to Elias Openshaw’s flight with its papers, and believes its most implacable members have pursued the family since.
snapshots.why: 129 names the Klan, 132 is the encyclopedia entry, 133 links it to Elias.

entities.notes: Kind is ‘group’, which is the final truth; if the UI displays kind on the first card, consider showing it neutrally, since Watson still treats K. K. K. as a ‘he’ at 112. Matching: the alias ends in a full stop and is followed by punctuation (’ , !), so a \b-based word-boundary matcher would miss it; match with non-word-character lookarounds. The bare letter ‘K’ (39 ‘the letter K three times’, 41 ‘treble K’, 115 ‘letter K of the American Encyclopædia’) is not bound. ‘the society’ (135) and ‘this gang’ (148) left unbound. Historical: the real Ku Klux Klan; the card follows the story’s own encyclopedia text.

entities.name: Captain James Calhoun
entities.subtitle: Captain of the barque Lone Star
entities.body: Captain of the American barque Lone Star, of Savannah, Georgia. Holmes addresses to him an envelope of five orange pips, marked ‘S. H. for J. O.’

snapshots.body: Captain of the barque Lone Star, of Savannah. Holmes calls him the leader of the gang behind the orange-pip warnings and sends him five pips of his own, signed ‘S. H. for J. O.’
snapshots.why: 165: ‘The leader of the gang.’

snapshots.body: Captain of the barque Lone Star, of Savannah, whom Holmes named as the gang’s leader. Holmes learned that he and his two mates were away from the ship on the night John Openshaw died and arranged for a murder charge to meet them in Savannah, but the Lone Star was apparently lost in the Atlantic gales and the pips never reached him.
snapshots.why: 176 (away from the ship; murder charge) and 177 (ship lost).

entities.notes: First mention is 162, the paragraph in which Holmes writes the address; the first card states only what 162 shows. His role is gated to 165. ‘Calhoun’ alone occurs only inside these two aliases. Left out of the cast-list threads because naming him at the start of the story would point to the solution.

entities.name: Lone Star
entities.subtitle: American barque out of Savannah, Georgia
entities.body: A barque (a sailing ship) whose home port is Savannah, Georgia.

aliasRules.why: Letters carved on the stern-post found in the Atlantic; the narration ties them to the Lone Star in the same sentence.

snapshots.body: An American barque out of Savannah. Holmes found that it called at Pondicherry early in 1883 and was at Dundee in January 1885, matching the postmarks of the first two orange-pip warnings.
snapshots.why: 168 and 172: the ship matches the Pondicherry and Dundee postmarks.

snapshots.body: An American barque out of Savannah, which Holmes traced to Pondicherry, Dundee and London when the orange-pip warnings were posted. It sailed for Savannah the morning after John Openshaw’s death and was apparently lost in that year’s gales; only a stern-post carved ‘L. S.’ was ever seen.
snapshots.why: 177: fate of the ship.

entities.notes: A ship, not a person. In both editions the name is italicised in the source text as ‘_Lone Star_’ (underscores are word characters, so ‘Lone Star’ with a \b matcher will not match; bind the underscored form, or ‘Lone Star’ if the matcher sees rendered text). Bound 6 times per edition (162, 168, 172, 174, 177×2). Texas is mentioned (169) as the ‘Lone Star’ state but not bound.

entities.name: Major Prendergast
entities.subtitle: Former client of Holmes who sends John to him
entities.body: An acquaintance of John Openshaw who told him about Holmes. Holmes had cleared him in the Tankerville Club scandal, when he was wrongly accused of cheating at cards.
entities.notes: Earlier case mentioned in passing (Tankerville Club scandal, 18–19). Appears only in John’s speech (18, 83).

entities.name: Major Freebody
entities.subtitle: Old friend of Joseph Openshaw at Portsdown Hill
entities.body: An old friend of Joseph Openshaw who commands one of the forts on Portsdown Hill, near Portsmouth. Joseph goes to stay with him.

aliasRules.why: Same paragraph, unambiguous: the major who telegraphs John.

entities.notes: Appears only at 64, which also narrates Joseph’s death; first card limited to the visit.

entities.name: Mr. Fordham
entities.subtitle: Horsham lawyer
entities.body: A lawyer (solicitor) in Horsham whom Elias Openshaw sends for to witness his will.

aliasRules.why: Same man, narration.
Same man, modern wording.

entities.notes: 40 ‘Fordham, the Horsham lawyer’; 42 ‘Mr. Fordham’.

entities.name: Mary
entities.subtitle: Member of Elias Openshaw’s household
entities.body: Someone in Elias Openshaw’s household at Horsham, apparently a servant, whom he wants told to light a fire in his room.
entities.notes: Mentioned once (40). The text does not state her role; ‘servant’ is hedged.

entities.name: Police-Constable Cook
entities.subtitle: Constable of the H Division
entities.body: A London police constable of the H Division, on duty near Waterloo Bridge, named in a newspaper report.
entities.notes: Only at 146, the paragraph reporting John’s death; card avoids what he heard.

entities.name: Hudson
entities.subtitle: Name on a page of Elias Openshaw’s diary
entities.body: A name in an entry dated 4 March 1869 on a torn page of Elias Openshaw’s diary: ‘Hudson came. Same old platform.’ The page does not say who he was.

aliasRules.why: Diary entry only. NOT Mrs. Hudson.

entities.notes: TRAP: not Mrs. Hudson (who is not mentioned in this story). Bound by paragraph rule only so a book-wide ‘Hudson’ alias can never reach it.

entities.name: McCauley
entities.subtitle: Name on a page of Elias Openshaw’s diary
entities.body: A name on a torn page of Elias Openshaw’s diary from March 1869: ‘Set the pips on McCauley, Paramore, and John Swain’, and two days later, ‘McCauley cleared.’

snapshots.body: A man named in Elias Openshaw’s 1869 diary. Holmes reads ‘set the pips on’ as sending him the society’s warning, and ‘McCauley cleared’ as meaning that he left the country.
snapshots.why: 135: Holmes interprets the diary page.

entities.name: Paramore
entities.subtitle: Name on a page of Elias Openshaw’s diary
entities.body: A name on a torn page of Elias Openshaw’s diary from March 1869: ‘Set the pips on McCauley, Paramore, and John Swain’, and later, ‘Visited Paramore. All well.’

snapshots.body: A man named in Elias Openshaw’s 1869 diary. Holmes reads the entries as meaning he received the society’s warning, did not leave, and was then ‘visited’, Holmes fears with a sinister result.
snapshots.why: 135: Holmes interprets ‘C was visited’.

entities.name: John Swain
entities.subtitle: Name on a page of Elias Openshaw’s diary
entities.body: A man ‘of St. Augustine’ named on a torn page of Elias Openshaw’s diary from March 1869: ‘Set the pips on … John Swain’, then ‘John Swain cleared.’

snapshots.body: A man of St. Augustine (Florida) named in Elias Openshaw’s 1869 diary. Holmes reads the entries as meaning he received the society’s warning and then left the country.
snapshots.why: 135: Holmes interprets the diary page.

entities.notes: Contains ‘John’; longer alias keeps him separate from John Openshaw.

entities.name: The Sholtos
entities.subtitle: Family from an earlier Holmes case
entities.body: A family from an earlier case of Holmes and Watson, the one Watson calls the Sign of Four. Holmes says John Openshaw faces even greater dangers than they did.
entities.notes: Earlier case mentioned (108–109). No facts imported from the novel.

entities.name: Clark Russell
entities.subtitle: Victorian writer of sea stories
entities.body: W. Clark Russell, a popular Victorian writer of sea stories; Watson is reading one of his books during the storm.

entities.name: Cuvier
entities.subtitle: French naturalist
entities.body: Georges Cuvier, the French naturalist, famous for reconstructing whole animals from single fossil bones; Holmes cites him as a model for reasoning.

entities.name: Lee
entities.subtitle: Confederate commander in the American Civil War
entities.body: Robert E. Lee, commander of the Confederate army, whose surrender in 1865 ended the American Civil War; John dates his uncle’s return to his plantation from it.
entities.notes: Text gives the surname only (35).

entities.name: Hood
entities.subtitle: Confederate general in the American Civil War
entities.body: A Confederate general, generally taken to be John Bell Hood, under whom Elias Openshaw served and rose to colonel.
entities.notes: Text gives the surname only (35); identification hedged.

entities.name: Jackson
entities.subtitle: Confederate general in the American Civil War
entities.body: A Confederate general in whose army Elias Openshaw first fought; usually taken to be Thomas ‘Stonewall’ Jackson.
entities.notes: Text gives the surname only (35); identification hedged.

entities.name: Isa Whitney
entities.subtitle: Opium addict and Watson’s patient
entities.body: Kate Whitney’s husband and one of Watson’s patients. He fell into opium addiction after trying to copy De Quincey’s accounts of opium dreams, and has been a slave to the drug for many years.
entities.notes: Bare ‘Whitney’ safe as an alias: ‘Kate Whitney’ and ‘Elias Whitney’ are longer matches and win. ‘Mr. Isa Whitney’ (16) is covered by ‘Isa Whitney’. ‘that sottish friend of yours’ (29) left unbound.

entities.name: Kate Whitney
entities.subtitle: Isa Whitney’s wife
entities.body: Isa Whitney’s wife and an old school friend of Watson’s wife. She arrives late at night, frightened, to ask the Watsons to bring her husband home from an opium den.

aliasRules.why: Watson speaking to Isa Whitney; ‘Your wife’ is unambiguously Kate.

entities.notes: ‘Kate’ occurs twice in 6 and twice in 24 (‘poor little Kate’).

entities.name: Elias Whitney
entities.subtitle: Isa Whitney’s late brother
entities.body: Isa Whitney’s late brother, a Doctor of Divinity who was Principal of the Theological College of St. George’s.
entities.notes: Mentioned once (paragraph 0).

entities.name: Thomas De Quincey
entities.subtitle: English essayist (1785–1859)
entities.body: English writer best known for Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1821). Isa Whitney read his description of his opium dreams and tried to reproduce them.
entities.notes: Real historical figure; text gives only the surname. ‘De Quincey’s’ matches via word boundary.

entities.name: Watson’s wife
entities.subtitle: Kate Whitney’s old school friend
entities.body: Watson’s wife, an old school friend of Kate Whitney. Friends in trouble tend to come to her for comfort.

aliasRules.why: Watson narrating about his own wife.
Modern edition starts the sentence with ‘My wife’.
Watson narrating about his own wife.
Holmes to Watson: send a note to your wife.

entities.notes: Never named in this story. ‘my wife’ must NOT be global: Neville St. Clair uses it for Mrs. St. Clair at 202 (M), 211, 212. She calls Watson ‘James’ at 8 (see recurring.watson).

entities.name: The Lascar
entities.subtitle: Manager of the Swandam Lane opium den
entities.body: The Lascar (an Indian sailor) who runs the Bar of Gold opium den in Upper Swandam Lane. Holmes calls him a rascal who has sworn revenge on him.

snapshots.body: The Lascar who runs the Bar of Gold opium den in Upper Swandam Lane, a man with a bad record. He blocked Mrs. St. Clair on the stairs when she tried to reach her husband. The police suspect he may have been an accomplice, but he says he knows nothing about the clothes or about his lodger, Hugh Boone.
snapshots.why: 60–62: he pushes Mrs. St. Clair out; police suspicion and his denial are reported.

snapshots.body: The Lascar who runs the Bar of Gold opium den. For a good rent he let Neville St. Clair use a room there to change into and out of his Hugh Boone disguise, and he was the only person who knew the secret. While the police were in the den, St. Clair secretly gave him the ring and a note for Mrs. St. Clair.
snapshots.why: 208 names him as the only man who knew the secret; 212 says St. Clair gave him the ring and note. Both come after the 195 reveal.

entities.notes: Only one Lascar in the story, so a global bare ‘Lascar’ is safe (it also covers ‘Lascar manager’, ‘Lascar confederate’, ‘Lascar scoundrel’). A ‘Dane’ assistant (60) and the ‘Malay attendant’ (15) are separate and left unbound. The trade term ‘Lascar’ is the only name the text gives him.

entities.name: Neville St. Clair
entities.subtitle: Mrs. St. Clair’s husband, of Lee in Kent
entities.body: A well-off gentleman of Lee, in Kent, who has gone missing. Holmes is investigating and fears he came to harm in the Swandam Lane opium den.

aliasRules.why: Inspector Bradstreet recognises the unmasked prisoner; after the 195 reveal.
After the reveal; the prisoner is now known to be St. Clair.
After the reveal.

snapshots.body: A well-off gentleman of Lee, in Kent, who has been missing since Monday. His wife saw him at a window of the Swandam Lane opium den, and his clothes were found in a room there. Now a note posted at Gravesend, which she is sure is in his hand, has reached her, telling her not to be frightened.
snapshots.why: 59–74 set out the disappearance; 102–121 bring the letter. No identity information.

snapshots.body: The missing gentleman of Lee, in Kent. In the Bow Street cells Holmes washes the face of the beggar Hugh Boone and reveals that the prisoner is Neville St. Clair himself, in disguise.
snapshots.why: 195: Holmes introduces the washed prisoner as ‘Mr. Neville St. Clair, of Lee’ — the identity reveal.

snapshots.body: A former actor and reporter who discovered that he could earn far more by begging in disguise as ‘Hugh Boone’ than by working. He kept up the double life for years without his wife knowing, until she saw him at the opium-den window. He has sworn never to play Hugh Boone again, and on that condition the police will probably keep the matter quiet.
snapshots.why: 206–212 confession; 218–219 Bradstreet’s condition and St. Clair’s oath.

entities.notes: Never bind Hugh Boone strings, ‘the cripple’, or ‘the prisoner’ before 195 to this entity. ‘Mr. St. Clair’ cannot match inside ‘Mrs. St. Clair’ (word boundary). ‘Mr. Neville St.—’ (199, cut off) matches only ‘Neville’. ‘NEVILLE’ is the letter’s signature (119). ‘her husband’, ‘the missing gentleman’ (62), ‘the man himself’ (M 68, M 211) left unbound.

entities.name: Mrs. St. Clair
entities.subtitle: Neville St. Clair’s wife
entities.body: Neville St. Clair’s wife, the daughter of a local brewer, who lives at The Cedars near Lee, in Kent. Her husband has disappeared, and Holmes is staying at her house while he investigates.

aliasRules.why: Holmes’s reconstruction: ‘when the wife tried to force her way up’.
St. Clair: ‘It was not the wife’ (original edition).
St. Clair: ‘It was not my wife’ (modern edition).
Holmes to St. Clair, after the reveal.
St. Clair’s confession, after the reveal.
Original edition only: ‘said the lady’ as she questions Holmes.

snapshots.body: Neville St. Clair’s wife, of The Cedars near Lee, in Kent. She saw her husband at a window in Swandam Lane on the day he vanished. She has now received a note posted at Gravesend which she is certain he wrote, and she is sure he is alive.
snapshots.why: 105–121: the letter.

entities.notes: First name never given. ‘this dear little woman’ (52) and ‘a little blonde woman’ (79) left unbound. Post-reveal ‘my wife’/‘your wife’/‘the wife’ in St. Clair’s and Holmes’s speech are bound by paragraph.

entities.name: Hugh Boone
entities.subtitle: The beggar with the twisted lip
entities.body: A disfigured professional beggar, well known in the City, who lodges in the Swandam Lane opium den where Neville St. Clair was last seen.

aliasRules.why: ‘the evident confusion which the cripple showed’ — the lodger, named as Hugh Boone at 62–63.
Same paragraph names him Hugh Boone.
Mrs. St. Clair refers to the lodger.
Mrs. St. Clair refers to the lodger.
Prisoner seen through the grating before the reveal — still Hugh Boone to the reader.
‘the prisoner’s face’ — before the reveal sentence in 195.

snapshots.body: A disfigured professional beggar, well known in the City, who lodges in the Swandam Lane opium den where Neville St. Clair was last seen. The police arrested him as a suspect in the disappearance; he denies ever having seen St. Clair.
snapshots.why: 67: Boone is arrested and searched.

snapshots.name: Hugh Boone (Neville St. Clair)
snapshots.body: ‘Hugh Boone’ was not a real person but a disguise. In the Bow Street cells Holmes washes off the beggar’s paint, scar and twisted lip and reveals the missing Neville St. Clair.
snapshots.why: 195: Holmes introduces the washed prisoner as Mr. Neville St. Clair.

snapshots.name: Hugh Boone (Neville St. Clair)
snapshots.body: The beggar persona that Neville St. Clair, a former actor, created with make-up, a red wig and a fake scar. Begging as Hugh Boone earned him far more than his old job as a reporter. He has now sworn that Hugh Boone will never appear again.
snapshots.why: 206–209 confession; 218–219 Bradstreet’s condition and the oath.

entities.notes: CRITICAL CONCEALMENT: separate entity from neville-st-clair. No pre-195 card or binding links the two. ‘a crippled wretch of hideous aspect’ (O 60) / ‘a hideous crippled wretch’ (M 60), ‘a cripple’ (64, 65 generic), ‘beggarman’ (175 — ‘Boone’ is bound there), ‘the sleeper’ (194) left unbound.

entities.name: Inspector Barton
entities.subtitle: Police inspector in the St. Clair case
entities.body: The police inspector in charge of the case after Neville St. Clair disappeared. He searched the premises at Swandam Lane.

aliasRules.why: ‘while the inspector remained upon the premises’ — Barton is named in the same paragraph.
‘The inspector stayed behind’ — Barton is named in the same paragraph.

entities.notes: The inspector Mrs. St. Clair meets in Fresno Street (60, 61) is probably Barton but the text does not say so, so those are left unbound.

entities.name: Inspector Bradstreet
entities.subtitle: Police inspector
entities.body: The police inspector on duty at the Bow Street police station, who knows Holmes. He is holding a prisoner Holmes wants to see.

aliasRules.why: Bradstreet sits at his desk.
Bradstreet in the Bow Street cells (Barton does not appear here).

snapshots.body: The police inspector on duty at the Bow Street police station, who knows Holmes. After the prisoner’s identity is revealed, he agrees the police can keep the affair quiet, as long as Hugh Boone never appears again.
snapshots.why: 218–220: Bradstreet’s condition and agreement; follows the 195 reveal.

snapshots.body: A police inspector who knows Holmes (an inspector Bradstreet handled the Hugh Boone affair). In the Hotel Cosmopolitan robbery he gave evidence at the police court about the arrest of John Horner.
snapshots.why: Newspaper report at 7:60.

snapshots.body: A police inspector, here of Scotland Yard (an inspector Bradstreet also appears at Bow Street in the Hugh Boone affair). He travels to Eyford with Holmes, Watson and Hatherley and draws a circle on the county map with Eyford at its centre to find the house.
snapshots.why: Introduced in story 9 at 9:137.

snapshots.body: A police inspector, here of Scotland Yard, who leads the search for the coining gang near Eyford. Watson says his confidence that they would be caught proved mistaken.
snapshots.why: 9:159 narrator foreshadows the failure.

entities.notes: SHARED id; first appearance in the collection (recurs in story 9). Subtitle kept generic (‘Police inspector’) so it stays true there. Not named Bradstreet until 170.

entities.name: Peterson
entities.subtitle: Commissionaire known to Holmes
entities.body: A commissionaire (a uniformed messenger) whom Holmes and Watson both know. He is the honest fellow who brought Holmes a stray hat and goose on Christmas morning.

aliasRules.why: “The commissionaire” / “the commissionaire” in these paragraphs is Peterson, named in 47 and 51; 6 and 47 already bind via “Peterson”.

snapshots.body: A commissionaire whom Holmes and Watson both know. He found a battered hat and a Christmas goose after a street scuffle, and his wife has now found a brilliant blue stone in the goose’s crop.
snapshots.why: Paragraph 50: Peterson brings in the blue stone his wife found in the goose.

entities.notes: His wife (50, “my wife”) and family (69, “your family”) are unnamed and unbound. 6 and 47 contain both “Peterson” and “the commissionaire”; only the name is bound there.

entities.name: Henry Baker
entities.subtitle: Owner of the lost hat and goose
entities.body: The man whose battered hat and Christmas goose Peterson picked up in Tottenham Court Road. All Holmes has to identify him are a card on the goose reading ‘For Mrs. Henry Baker’ and the initials ‘H. B.’ in the hat.

aliasRules.why: “said Baker” — bare “Baker” only here; elsewhere bare “Baker” is “Baker Street” (63, 79, 170) or “Bakers” in 12.
Unambiguously Henry Baker in Holmes’s room.
Same sentence in the modern edition.
Unambiguously Henry Baker.

exclude.why: Inside the card text “For Mrs. Henry Baker”, which names his wife, not him.

snapshots.body: A down-at-heel scholarly man who reclaims his hat and happily takes a replacement goose. He got his bird through the goose club at the Alpha Inn, and Holmes is satisfied that he knows nothing about the stone.
snapshots.why: 93 gives the Alpha goose club; 94 Holmes declares he knows nothing of the matter.

entities.notes: First textual appearance is the card “For Mrs. Henry Baker” in 12 (excluded). “Henry Bakers” in 12 does not match (word boundary). The tall man in a Scotch bonnet at 79 is Baker but is left unbound (named in 80). Holmes’s initial suspicion question (73–74) is attributed; he is never a culprit.

entities.name: John Horner
entities.subtitle: Plumber charged with the jewel robbery
entities.body: A plumber accused of stealing the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. The evidence against him is strong enough that the case has been sent to the Assizes.

snapshots.body: A 26-year-old plumber charged with stealing the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. The police case against him is described as strong, and he has a previous conviction, but he protests his innocence.
snapshots.why: Newspaper report details complete at 7:60.

snapshots.body: The plumber charged with the jewel robbery. Holmes establishes that he was deliberately set up: called to the Countess’s room so that suspicion would fall on him, for a crime he knew nothing about.
snapshots.why: 183 Holmes lays out how Horner was made the scapegoat; 185 states he knew nothing of the crime.

snapshots.body: The plumber wrongly charged with the jewel robbery. Holmes expects the case against him to collapse because the real thief will not appear against him.
snapshots.why: 213: Holmes says the witness will not appear and the case must collapse.

entities.notes: First card attributes the charge and does not assert guilt or innocence.

entities.name: Catherine Cusack
entities.subtitle: Maid to the Countess of Morcar
entities.body: The Countess of Morcar’s maid. At the police court she testified that she heard the cry of alarm when the robbery was discovered and rushed into the room.
