snapshots.body: The Countess of Morcar’s maid. Ryder says it was she who told him about the blue stone, and Holmes names her as his confederate in arranging the job that put the plumber Horner in the room.
snapshots.why: 182 Ryder says Cusack told him of the stone; 183 Holmes calls her his confederate.

entities.notes: “her ladyship’s waiting-maid” (183 O) / “Her ladyship’s maid” (183 M) also denote her but are left unbound (generic, and inside the reveal paragraph).

entities.name: Countess of Morcar
entities.subtitle: Owner of the blue carbuncle
entities.body: A titled lady whose famous blue carbuncle was stolen from her jewel-case at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. She has offered a £1,000 reward for its return.
entities.notes: Mentioned only; never appears. “the lady’s jewel-case” (59 O), “my lady’s room” and “her ladyship’s” (183) left unbound as generic.

entities.name: Windigate
entities.subtitle: Landlord of the Alpha Inn
entities.body: The landlord of the Alpha Inn, a small Bloomsbury pub near the British Museum. This year he ran a goose club for his regulars, who paid a few pence a week for a Christmas bird.

aliasRules.why: “our excellent landlord, Windigate” (93 M) and “The landlord looked startled” (100 M) — the Alpha’s landlord.
The Alpha’s landlord, Windigate (named in 93 and 147).

entities.notes: Holmes never learns his name from him directly; the reader learns it from Baker in 93. “our good host” (93 O) left unbound.

entities.name: Breckinridge
entities.subtitle: Goose salesman at Covent Garden Market
entities.body: A poultry salesman at Covent Garden Market who supplied the Alpha Inn with its two dozen geese.

aliasRules.why: “a salesman in Covent Garden” and “the salesman” in these paragraphs are Breckinridge. 163 is covered by his name.
Modern rendering of “salesman” in the same paragraphs. NOT 105 M (“a few dealers there”) or 202–203 (Maggie’s generic “the dealer”).

snapshots.body: A sharp-faced, short-tempered poultry salesman with one of the largest stalls in Covent Garden Market. He refuses to say where the Alpha’s geese came from, but Holmes provokes him into a bet and he shows his ledger: they came from Mrs. Oakshott of Brixton Road.
snapshots.why: Holmes explains the betting trick at 7:150.

entities.notes: Named by the landlord in 106. Calls Holmes “Mr. Cocksure” (138 O) / “Mr. Know-it-all” (138 M).

entities.name: Bill
entities.subtitle: Boy at Breckinridge’s stall
entities.body: The boy who helps at Breckinridge’s poultry stall in Covent Garden. Breckinridge sends him to fetch the account books.
entities.notes: Also the unnamed “a boy” (109) and “The small boy” / “The boy” (137); left unbound as generic.

entities.name: Mrs. Oakshott
entities.subtitle: Egg and poultry supplier in Brixton Road
entities.body: An egg and poultry supplier at 117 Brixton Road. Breckinridge’s ledger shows she sold him twenty-four geese on 22 December.

aliasRules.why: Ryder’s sister, who married Oakshott and fattens geese in Brixton Road (stated in 188).
Capitalised variant, same person.

snapshots.body: James Ryder’s sister, married to a man named Oakshott. She fattens fowls for the market at 117 Brixton Road and sold Breckinridge twenty-four geese on 22 December.
snapshots.why: Ryder names his sister at 7:188.

snapshots.body: James Ryder’s sister, married to a man named Oakshott. She fattens geese for the market in Brixton Road and had promised her brother a goose for Christmas.
snapshots.why: 188: Ryder says his sister married Oakshott and fattens fowls in Brixton Road; 190 adds the promised Christmas goose. Gate moved to 190, where the promised goose is first mentioned.

snapshots.body: James Ryder’s sister, married to a man named Oakshott. She fattens geese for the market in Brixton Road and had promised her brother a goose for Christmas. Ryder calls her Maggie.
snapshots.why: Name Maggie first at 7:194.

entities.notes: Ryder calls her “Maggie” (194, 201), both after the 188 reveal. The snapshot mentions the promised goose (190) slightly early; if strict gating is wanted, move the snapshot to [7, 190]. Her husband (“a man named Oakshott”, 188) is unbound: bare “Oakshott” is not an alias.

entities.name: James Ryder
entities.subtitle: Upper attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan
entities.body: An upper attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. He testified that he showed the plumber Horner up to the Countess of Morcar’s dressing-room, was called away, and raised the alarm when he found her jewel-case empty.

aliasRules.why: His sister’s pet name for him in his own story (191–206), all after his identity is revealed in 168.
Ryder in Holmes’s room, after his real name is given in 168.

snapshots.body: An upper attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan who testified about the jewel robbery. He has turned up at Covent Garden under the name “John Robinson”, desperate to trace a goose sold through Breckinridge’s stall.
snapshots.why: 168: the little man at the stall gives his real name, James Ryder, after first saying “John Robinson” (166).

snapshots.body: An upper attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. Holmes exposes him as the thief of the blue carbuncle: with the maid Catherine Cusack he arranged for Horner, a man with a previous conviction, to be called to the room, then emptied the jewel-case and raised the alarm.
snapshots.why: 179 “The game’s up, Ryder”; 183 Holmes sets out how the theft and frame-up were done.

snapshots.body: The hotel attendant who stole the blue carbuncle and let Horner be blamed. He hid the stone in a goose at his sister’s, took the wrong bird, and lost track of it. Holmes lets him go: without Ryder’s evidence the case against Horner must collapse, and Holmes judges him too frightened to go wrong again.
snapshots.why: 188–207 his confession; 209–212 Holmes sends him away; 213 Holmes explains why.

entities.notes: Gated: (1) that the rat-faced man at Breckinridge’s stall is Ryder (151–168, revealed 168); (2) his guilt (179/183); (3) outcome (212–213). Before 168 the little man is never bound (“a little rat-faced fellow”, “the little man”, “the inquirer”, “the stranger” all unbound). The 60 card reports only his public testimony.

entities.name: John Robinson
entities.subtitle: Name given by the man asking after geese
entities.body: The name given by the anxious little man who was pestering Breckinridge about geese, when Holmes asks whom he is helping.

snapshots.name: John Robinson (false name)
snapshots.body: A false name. Pressed by Holmes, the man admits his real name is James Ryder, an attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan.
snapshots.why: 167 Holmes calls it an alias; 168 the real name James Ryder is given.

entities.notes: Own entity per the alias rule; never bound to james-ryder.

entities.name: Maudsley
entities.subtitle: Ryder’s friend in Kilburn
entities.body: A friend of James Ryder’s who went to the bad and has just served a sentence in Pentonville. He lives in Kilburn, and Ryder hoped he would help turn the stolen stone into money.

aliasRules.why: “I told my pal what I had done” — Maudsley.
Modern rendering of “my pal” — Maudsley. (Elsewhere “my friend” is Holmes, via Watson.)

entities.notes: Mentioned only, inside Ryder’s confession; the card is first shown after Ryder’s guilt is already revealed (183), so naming the stolen stone is safe.

entities.name: Helen Stoner
entities.subtitle: Holmes’s client; Julia Stoner’s twin sister
entities.body: A frightened young woman who arrives at Baker Street early in the morning to ask Holmes for help. She lives with her stepfather, Dr. Grimesby Roylott, at the old family house of Stoke Moran in Surrey.

aliasRules.why: Holmes addresses Helen as ‘Miss Roylott’ here (both editions); unambiguous.
Unambiguously Helen, after she has given her name.
Modern edition only (‘looked towards our visitor’); original has ‘his visitor’.

snapshots.body: Holmes’s client, a woman of about thirty whose twin sister Julia died at Stoke Moran two years ago. Now engaged to Percy Armitage, she has been moved into Julia’s old room during repairs, and last night she heard the same low whistle that came before her sister’s death.
snapshots.why: 66: engagement, move into Julia’s room, the whistle heard again.

snapshots.body: Holmes’s client from Stoke Moran. After the night’s events and her stepfather’s death, Holmes and Watson take her by the morning train to her aunt at Harrow.
snapshots.why: 246: aftermath; she is taken to her aunt. Roylott’s death already revealed at 241–244.

entities.notes: Unnamed before 21 (‘a young lady’, ‘the woman’, ‘our visitor’ at 19) – left unbound. Para 0 mentions ‘the untimely death of the lady to whom the pledge was given’; the text never says this is Helen, so it is left unbound and her card never mentions it. Counts: O = Helen Stoner 2 (incl. ‘Miss Helen Stoner’ at 89) + Helen 2 + Miss Stoner 15 + Miss Roylott 1 + our visitor 1; M = 2 + 2 + 14 + 1 + 2.

entities.name: Julia Stoner
entities.subtitle: Helen Stoner’s twin sister
entities.body: Helen Stoner’s twin sister, who grew up with her under Dr. Roylott’s roof at Stoke Moran.

snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s twin sister. She died two years ago at Stoke Moran, aged thirty, within a fortnight of her planned wedding to a major of marines she had met at her aunt’s.
snapshots.why: 27–29: Helen reveals Julia’s death two years ago and the engagement.

snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s twin sister. Two years ago, shortly before her wedding, she had been hearing a low whistle at night. On a stormy night Helen heard her scream; Julia staggered out of her room, cried ‘It was the band! The speckled band!’ and died without regaining consciousness.
snapshots.why: 35–49: the whistle conversation and the night of her death; the coroner’s finding follows at 55 but is general setup. Card quotes her words without interpreting them.

snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s twin sister. Two years ago, shortly before her wedding, she had been hearing a low whistle at night. On a stormy night Helen heard her scream; Julia staggered out of her room, cried ‘It was the band! The speckled band!’ and died without regaining consciousness. The coroner could find no cause of death: her door and shutters were fastened, there were no marks of violence and no trace of poison. Helen believes she died of fright.
snapshots.why: Inquest findings 8:55–59.

snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s twin sister. Holmes concludes she was killed by a swamp adder that her stepfather sent through the ventilator and down the false bell-rope onto her bed; ‘the band’ was her description of the snake glimpsed by matchlight.
snapshots.why: 247: Holmes explains the mechanism of Julia’s death.

entities.notes: Only named three times; usually ‘my sister’ / ‘your sister’ / ‘her sister’ / ‘the dying woman’, which are left unbound (generic, and several occurrences refer to Helen’s grief rather than naming Julia). Never called ‘Miss Stoner’ in the text.

entities.subtitle: Helen Stoner’s stepfather, of Stoke Moran
entities.body: A doctor and the last of the ancient Roylott family of Stoke Moran in Surrey. He is the stepfather of Helen Stoner, who lives with him in the old family house.

aliasRules.why: Holmes addresses him as ‘Doctor’.
Original edition lowercase ‘the doctor’ = Roylott (modern has ‘the Doctor’). 217 ‘a doctor’ is generic and not bound.

snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s stepfather, last of the ruined Roylotts. He practised medicine in Calcutta, served a long prison term after beating his native butler to death, and married Helen’s widowed mother in India. Back at Stoke Moran he is feared for his violent temper, befriends only the wandering gipsies, and keeps a cheetah and a baboon.
snapshots.why: 23–26: Helen’s account of his past and character.

snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s stepfather, a violent man who burst into Baker Street to threaten Holmes. Holmes has read his late wife’s will and finds that the stepdaughters’ marriages would sharply cut his income, which Holmes regards as a strong motive to prevent them.
snapshots.why: 94–114: confrontation (110) and the will (114). Holmes’s suspicion is attributed, not asserted.

snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s stepfather. Holmes and Watson find him dead in his room, killed within seconds by a swamp adder coiled round his head; Holmes calls him a schemer who has fallen into the pit he dug for another.
snapshots.why: 241–244: discovery of his death and of the snake.

snapshots.body: Helen Stoner’s stepfather. Holmes concludes that he killed Julia by sending a trained swamp adder through the ventilator and down a false bell-rope, recalling it with a whistle, and that Helen, moved into the same room, was next. Holmes’s blows drove the snake back through the ventilator, and it turned on Roylott.
snapshots.why: 247–250: Holmes’s full explanation.

entities.notes: Para 0 already mentions rumours about his death; the first card deliberately omits this. The huge man at 94–96 (‘a huge man’, ‘this apparition’, ‘this formidable figure’) is left unbound until he names himself at 97. ‘the dead man’ (245) unbound. Counts O: Dr. Grimesby Roylott 8, Dr. Roylott 11, the Doctor 5, the doctor 3, Doctor 1, stepfather forms 12, the old man 2. M: 7, 12, 8, 0, 1, 12, 2.

entities.name: Mrs. Stoner
entities.subtitle: Helen and Julia Stoner’s mother
entities.body: Helen and Julia Stoner’s mother, the young widow of Major-General Stoner of the Bengal Artillery, who married Dr. Roylott in India.

snapshots.body: Helen and Julia Stoner’s mother, who married Dr. Roylott in India. She was killed eight years ago in a railway accident near Crewe. Her income of at least £1000 a year went to Dr. Roylott while her daughters lived with him, with a yearly sum reserved for each daughter on marriage.
snapshots.why: 24 reveals her death and the terms of her will.

snapshots.body: Helen and Julia Stoner’s mother, killed eight years ago in a railway accident. Holmes finds that her will now yields about £750 a year, of which each daughter may claim £250 on marriage.
snapshots.why: 114: Holmes reads the will.

entities.notes: Otherwise ‘my mother’ (24, 29) and ‘the deceased wife’ / ‘his late wife’ (114) – left unbound as generic.

entities.name: Major-General Stoner
entities.subtitle: Helen and Julia Stoner’s late father
entities.body: An officer of the Bengal Artillery, the first husband of Mrs. Stoner and father of the twins Helen and Julia. He had died before his widow remarried in India.
entities.notes: Mentioned once. Father relationship is implied by ‘young widow of Major-General Stoner’ and the shared surname of the twins.

entities.name: Miss Honoria Westphail
entities.subtitle: Helen and Julia Stoner’s aunt, near Harrow
entities.body: The unmarried sister of Helen and Julia’s mother, living near Harrow. The sisters were sometimes allowed short visits to her house.

aliasRules.why: ‘an aunt’ (29), ‘your aunt’ (130), ‘her good/kindly aunt’ (246) all denote her.

snapshots.body: Helen and Julia’s maternal aunt near Harrow. Holmes and Watson bring Helen to her care after the night at Stoke Moran.
snapshots.why: 246: Helen is taken to her aunt.

entities.notes: First bound span is ‘aunt’ earlier in 29, immediately followed by the full name in the same sentence.

entities.name: Julia’s fiancé
entities.subtitle: Julia Stoner’s fiancé, a major of marines
entities.body: A half-pay major of marines whom Julia Stoner met at her aunt’s at Christmas two years ago and became engaged to. He is never named.

aliasRules.why: Original ‘a half-pay major of marines’, modern ‘a major of marines on half-pay’; both contain this span.

entities.notes: Optional minor card; can be dropped to unbound if the book prefers no unnamed one-offs.

entities.name: Percy Armitage
entities.subtitle: Helen Stoner’s fiancé
entities.body: A dear friend of Helen Stoner’s for many years and the second son of Mr. Armitage of Crane Water, near Reading. He proposed to Helen a month ago, and they plan to marry in the spring.

aliasRules.why: First bare ‘Armitage’ (‘His name is Armitage—Percy Armitage’) is Percy; the other bare-surname match is inside ‘Mr. Armitage’, which is claimed by the longer alias of mr-armitage.

entities.notes: Helen’s ‘one, who cares for me … he, poor fellow, can be of little aid’ (16) and ‘he to whom of all others I have a right to look for help’ (19) very probably mean Percy, but the text never confirms it; left unbound.

entities.name: Mr. Armitage
entities.subtitle: Percy Armitage’s father, of Crane Water
entities.body: The father of Helen Stoner’s fiancé, Percy Armitage; he lives at Crane Water, near Reading.
entities.notes: Exists mainly so that the span ‘Mr. Armitage’ is not bound to Percy via the bare surname.

entities.name: Mrs. Farintosh
entities.subtitle: A former client of Holmes
entities.body: A woman whom Holmes once helped in a time of great need. She told Helen Stoner about him and gave her his address.

snapshots.body: A former client of Holmes who recommended him to Helen Stoner. According to his case-book, her case concerned an opal tiara and came before Watson’s time.
snapshots.why: 18: Holmes recalls the opal tiara case.

entities.notes: Earlier, unrecorded case. Nothing beyond 16 and 18 is known; do not import details.

entities.name: The gipsies
entities.subtitle: Travellers camped on the Stoke Moran estate
entities.body: Wandering gipsies whom Dr. Roylott allows to camp on the bramble-covered remnant of his estate. They are his only friends, and he sometimes travels with them for weeks.

snapshots.body: Gipsies camped in the plantation at Stoke Moran, friends of Dr. Roylott. Helen has wondered whether her sister’s dying words about ‘a band’ meant these people, many of whom wear spotted handkerchiefs on their heads.
snapshots.why: 60–63: Helen’s speculation linking them to ‘the band’ (attributed).

snapshots.body: Gipsies camped on Dr. Roylott’s land. Holmes later admits that their presence, together with the word ‘band’, first put him on an entirely wrong scent.
snapshots.why: 247: Holmes says the gipsy theory was mistaken.

entities.notes: Modern 89 uses ‘the gipsy band’s’ (alias ‘gipsy’); original 89 ‘a band of gipsies’. Never bind ‘band’ to them.

entities.name: The cheetah
entities.subtitle: Dr. Roylott’s Indian animal
entities.body: One of the Indian animals sent to Dr. Roylott by a correspondent. It roams freely over the grounds of Stoke Moran, and the villagers fear it almost as much as its master.
entities.notes: 166 ‘a cheetah is just a big cat’ is a general remark but about this animal; harmless to bind.

entities.name: The baboon
entities.subtitle: Dr. Roylott’s Indian animal
entities.body: One of the Indian animals sent to Dr. Roylott by a correspondent. It wanders freely over the grounds of Stoke Moran and frightens the villagers.

snapshots.body: Dr. Roylott’s free-roaming baboon. At night it darts out of the laurels on the lawn like a ‘hideous and distorted child’, startling Holmes and Watson.
snapshots.why: 221–224: the figure on the lawn is identified as the baboon.

entities.notes: 221 ‘a hideous and distorted child’ is left unbound (identified only at 224).

entities.name: Swamp adder
entities.subtitle: Venomous Indian snake
entities.body: A venomous snake that Holmes finds in Dr. Roylott’s room at the climax and names as the deadliest snake in India.

aliasRules.why: After the reveal at 244 only. Modern 243 ‘snake’s’ (before the naming) and original 243 ‘serpent’ stay unbound.
Modern ‘the snake’s neck’ (original has ‘reptile’s’).

snapshots.body: The venomous snake behind the ‘speckled band’. Holmes concludes Dr. Roylott had trained it, probably with milk, to come back at his whistle, and sent it through the ventilator and down the false bell-rope onto the bed.
snapshots.why: 247–250: Holmes’s explanation.

snapshots.body: The venomous snake behind the ‘speckled band’. Holmes concludes Dr. Roylott had trained it, probably with milk, to come back at his whistle, and sent it through the ventilator and down the false bell-rope onto the bed. Holmes’s cane drove it back through the ventilator, where it turned on its master.
snapshots.why: Holmes explains at 8:249–250.

entities.notes: THE SOLUTION. Card exists only from 244. Never bind ‘band’, ‘the speckled band’ (49, 62, 242), ‘yellow band’ (241), ‘strange headgear’ (243), ‘serpent’ (243), ‘creature’, ‘something’ or ‘it’. Counts O: swamp adder 1 + snake 3 (244, 247×2); M: 1 + 4 (244, 245, 247×2).

entities.name: The Roylotts of Stoke Moran
entities.subtitle: Old Saxon family of Stoke Moran, Surrey
entities.body: One of the oldest Saxon families in England, whose ancestral house is Stoke Moran on the western border of Surrey.

aliasRules.why: ‘a Roylott (of Stoke Moran)’ = a member of the family. Elsewhere bare ‘Roylott’ is always inside a longer alias (‘Dr. Roylott’, ‘Miss Roylott’).

snapshots.body: An ancient Saxon family of Stoke Moran, once among the richest in England, ruined by four wasteful heirs and a Regency gambler. Only a few acres and a mortgaged two-hundred-year-old house remain; a violent temper runs in the family’s men.
snapshots.why: 23–25: Helen’s history of the family.

entities.notes: Optional family card.

entities.name: Palmer
entities.subtitle: Victorian doctor turned murderer
entities.body: A real doctor turned criminal whom Holmes cites as an example of medical men who became leading criminals. Generally identified as William Palmer, the Rugeley poisoner hanged in 1856.
entities.notes: Text gives surname only; full identification is standard historical annotation, not from the story.

entities.name: Pritchard
entities.subtitle: Victorian doctor turned murderer
entities.body: A real doctor turned criminal whom Holmes cites alongside Palmer. Generally identified as Dr. Edward William Pritchard, the Glasgow poisoner hanged in 1865.
entities.notes: Text gives surname only; full identification is standard historical annotation.

entities.name: Victor Hatherley
entities.subtitle: Young London hydraulic engineer
entities.body: A young hydraulic engineer with offices in Victoria Street, London. His case reaches Holmes through Watson, who treats him early one morning for a badly injured hand.

aliasRules.why: Watson’s narration (‘my visitor’s name’) refers to Hatherley; modern edition only.
‘answered my visitor’ is Hatherley.

Same sentence in the modern edition.

Hatherley questions the station-master.
Modern edition: ‘How the engineer reached…’.
Original edition: ‘How our hydraulic engineer…’.
Hatherley’s closing lament.

snapshots.body: A young hydraulic engineer hired by Colonel Lysander Stark for a secret night’s work at a country house reached by carriage from Eyford station. At the house he was locked inside a hydraulic press, escaped through a panel with a woman’s help, and lost his thumb to the colonel’s cleaver while hanging from a window. He woke near Eyford station and has put the case in Holmes’s hands.
snapshots.why: Paragraphs 119–132 give his full account of the attack and escape.

entities.notes: Name aliases: original 8 (0, 8, 40, 46×2, 83, 154, 169), modern 7 (46 has one ‘Mr. Hatherley’ in modern). Rule-bound descriptions add 11 (original) / 12 (modern). The thumb injury is in the story title and at paragraphs 14–15, so the first card can mention a hand injury; who did it is gated. ‘hydraulic engineer’ at 8 and 43 is his job title, not bound separately (inside the card text / self-description).

entities.name: Colonel Lysander Stark
entities.subtitle: Hatherley’s secretive client
entities.body: An extremely thin man, nearer forty than thirty, with a slight German accent. He calls at Hatherley’s office with a card engraved ‘Colonel Lysander Stark’ and brings a commission that he insists must stay secret.

aliasRules.why: Every lowercase ‘the colonel’ from 45 to 136 is Stark. Colonel Warburton (0) is always ‘Colonel Warburton’.
Sentence-initial variant in the modern edition (45, 95, 96, 136).
Hatherley shouts ‘Colonel! Let me out!’ at Stark.
The woman cries ‘Fritz! Fritz!’ while holding Stark back. The paragraph itself makes it plain who she is addressing. Bound only here.
Narrator’s summary of the vanished trio; refers to Stark.

snapshots.body: The thin, German-accented man who hired Hatherley under the name Colonel Lysander Stark. When Hatherley saw through the fuller’s-earth story, Stark locked him inside the hydraulic press and set it going. He then pursued him with a cleaver and cut off his thumb at the window. Elise, the woman at the house, calls him ‘Fritz’; whether either name is his real one is not yet clear.
snapshots.why: 119–120: he locks Hatherley in the press; 126–128: cleaver attack, and the woman calls him ‘Fritz’.

snapshots.body: The thin, German-accented man who hired Hatherley as Colonel Lysander Stark and tried to kill him in the hydraulic press. Holmes suspects he did the same to a missing engineer, Jeremiah Hayling, a year earlier. Holmes concludes that Stark’s group are large-scale coiners who use the press to make false silver; the police had already been hunting such a gang. The woman called him ‘Fritz’.
snapshots.why: 134: Holmes links him to Hayling; 157–158: the coining gang is identified.

snapshots.body: The thin, German-accented man who hired Hatherley as Colonel Lysander Stark and tried to kill him in the hydraulic press. Holmes identifies him as one of a large-scale coining gang. He escaped before the police arrived, and Watson says nothing has been heard of ‘the sinister German’ since. His real name is never established; the woman called him ‘Fritz’.
snapshots.why: 159 foreshadows the escape; 171 states the gang vanished and was never traced.

entities.notes: Name aliases 9 per edition (45, 95×2, 96, 97, 104, 113, 126, 131). The modern edition uses ‘Colonel Stark’ where the original has ‘Colonel Lysander Stark’ at 95 (second), 104, 113 and 126. ‘the colonel’/‘The colonel’ 10 per edition, plus ‘Colonel’ (119), ‘Fritz’ ×2 (127) and ‘the sinister German’ (171). The text never says whether ‘Lysander Stark’ or ‘Fritz’ is his real name, and the porter does not recognise the name (131). The station-master’s ‘foreign gentleman… a patient’ staying with Dr. Becher (167) matches his description, but the text does not say so outright, so that phrase is left unbound. I did not bind a few loose epithets: ‘my patron’ (86 O) / ‘my client’ (86 M), ‘my acquaintance of the morning’ (87), ‘my companion’ (96), ‘the ruffian’ (126 O) / ‘the brute’ (126 M) and ‘the villain’ (142). They are safe to bind to Stark if wanted.

entities.name: The woman at the house
entities.subtitle: Foreign woman in Colonel Stark’s house
entities.body: A pretty, frightened woman in a rich dark dress who appears with a lamp at the house where Colonel Stark brings Hatherley. She speaks to the colonel in a foreign language.

aliasRules.why: Her first appearance with the lamp.
She comes to Hatherley’s room.
Hatherley wonders if she is a monomaniac.
Same, lowercase in modern.
‘the warnings of the lady’.
‘the woman’s warning’.

Same, sentence-initial in modern.
Hatherley: ‘what the girl said’.
Unambiguous references to her.
Unambiguous references to her.
Narrator’s summary of the vanished trio.

snapshots.body: A pretty, frightened woman at the house where Colonel Stark brings Hatherley. She slips into his room and begs him in broken English to leave before it is too late. He refuses, half suspecting she is unbalanced.
snapshots.why: 99–103: her warning.

snapshots.name: Elise
snapshots.body: The woman at the house where Hatherley was taken. After warning him to leave, she opened a panel that let him escape the hydraulic press and led him to a bedroom window. She tried to hold back the man she calls ‘Fritz’ (Colonel Stark), reminding him of a promise ‘after the last time’. He calls her Elise.
snapshots.why: 121–122: rescue; 127–128: she pleads with ‘Fritz’ and is named Elise.

snapshots.name: Elise
snapshots.body: The woman who warned Hatherley and helped him escape the hydraulic press. She vanished with the gang and was never heard of again. Footprints suggest she and the Englishman probably carried the unconscious Hatherley away from the house to safety.
snapshots.why: 171: the trio vanish; 173: the footprint inference (stated as ‘most probable’).

entities.notes: Named only at 128 (‘Elise’). Her relationship to Stark (wife, sister, etc.) is never stated, so don’t claim one. ‘the girl’ at 135 is original-only; modern says ‘the woman’s words’. I did not bind the epithets ‘the same good friend’ (122 O) / ‘kind protector’ (122 M), ‘My guide’ (124) and ‘my saviour’ (126 O) / ‘my rescuer’ (126 M); they are safe to add.

entities.name: Mr. Ferguson
entities.subtitle: Introduced as Stark’s secretary and manager
entities.body: A short, stout, silent Englishman with a chinchilla beard. Colonel Stark introduces him to Hatherley as his secretary and manager.

aliasRules.why: ‘the fat manager and I’ = Ferguson (introduced as manager at 105).
Modern wording of the same.
112 establishes Ferguson as the ‘morose and silent’ fellow-countryman.
Modern wording; 112 M calls Ferguson ‘surly and taciturn’.
Same man.
Same man.

snapshots.body: A short, stout, silent Englishman introduced as Colonel Stark’s secretary and manager. He helped show Hatherley the hydraulic press, which Holmes concludes was used by a large-scale coining gang.
snapshots.why: 157: Holmes identifies the coining operation.

snapshots.body: A short, stout, silent Englishman introduced as Colonel Stark’s secretary and manager. He vanished with the coining gang and was never traced. Footprints suggest he probably helped the woman carry the unconscious Hatherley to safety, being ‘less bold or less murderous’ than Stark.
snapshots.why: 171: vanished; 173: footprint inference.

entities.notes: Name aliases 4 per edition (104, 107, 112, 113). ‘was introduced to me as Mr. Ferguson’, so Ferguson may not be his real name; the card says ‘introduced as’. The text never identifies him with Dr. Becher (see becher notes).

entities.name: Dr. Becher
entities.subtitle: Named by the Eyford station-master
entities.body: A local doctor. The Eyford station-master names him as the owner of a house that caught fire during the night.

snapshots.body: A local doctor, named by the Eyford station-master as the owner of the burning house. The station-master describes him as a well-fed Englishman with a foreign gentleman, said to be a patient, staying with him. Hatherley recognises the burning house as the one where he was attacked. Hatherley’s question shows he suspects the thin foreign ‘patient’ is the man who hired him. The story never says whether Becher himself is one of the people Hatherley met there.
snapshots.why: 165–167: station-master’s description; 169: Hatherley identifies the house.

entities.notes: Mentioned only; never appears. 166: in the original, Hatherley asks ‘is Dr. Becher a German…?’; modern says ‘is he…?’, so modern has one fewer mention. What the text settles: the house is Becher’s (165) and it is the house where Hatherley was attacked (169). What it does NOT settle: whether Becher is Ferguson (both are stout Englishmen) or otherwise part of the gang. Whether his ‘foreign’ patient is Stark is implied but not stated. Don’t assert either; the 169 snapshot leaves it explicitly open. Watson is also called ‘Doctor’/‘the doctor’ in this story; Becher is always ‘Dr. Becher’, so there are no span collisions.

entities.name: Jeremiah Hayling
entities.subtitle: Missing hydraulic engineer in an old advertisement
entities.body: A twenty-six-year-old hydraulic engineer reported missing in a newspaper advertisement Holmes kept from about a year earlier. He left his lodgings at ten at night and had not been heard of since.

snapshots.body: A twenty-six-year-old hydraulic engineer who vanished about a year earlier after leaving his lodgings at night. Holmes suspects that ‘the colonel’ had called him in to service the same machine.
snapshots.why: 134 (end): Holmes’s inference linking Hayling to the colonel.

entities.notes: Holmes’s link to the colonel is an inference (‘I fancy’ / ‘I suspect’), so the snapshot attributes it to Holmes. Hatherley’s reaction (135) connects it to Elise’s ‘after the last time’ (127).

entities.name: The railway guard
entities.subtitle: Paddington railway guard, Watson’s former patient
entities.body: A railway guard from Paddington whom Watson once treated. He has been sending Watson patients ever since, and this morning he brings one to Watson’s door himself.

aliasRules.why: ‘my old ally, the guard’.
Watson’s epithet for the guard.
Modern wording of the same.
Hatherley describes the man who escorted him from Paddington.
Modern wording of the same.

entities.subtitle: Station-master at Eyford
entities.body: The station-master at Eyford, who answers Bradstreet’s questions about a house fire visible from the station.

aliasRules.why: Answers Bradstreet.
Describes Dr. Becher.
Original only; modern says ‘Before he had finished’.

entities.name: The plain-clothes man
entities.subtitle: Plain-clothes policeman with Bradstreet
entities.body: A plain-clothes policeman who travels to Eyford with Inspector Bradstreet, Holmes, Watson and Hatherley.

Modern wording.
Votes for west.
Modern wording.

entities.name: Lord Robert St. Simon
entities.subtitle: Holmes’s noble client; second son of the Duke of Balmoral
entities.body: An aristocrat of forty-one, second son of the Duke of Balmoral and a former Under-Secretary for the colonies. He writes to Holmes about a painful event connected with his wedding.
aliases: Lord Robert Walsingham de Vere St. Simon

aliasRules.why: Hatty addresses him by first name; elsewhere 'Robert' only occurs inside longer full-name matches.
Unambiguously Lord St. Simon in these paragraphs ('our client' in 136 is original-en only).
Narration naming Lord St. Simon.
Holmes on the letter-writer.
Narration.
Modern-en narration/speech for Lord St. Simon.

snapshots.body: An aristocrat of forty-one, second son of the Duke of Balmoral. His American bride, Hatty Doran, vanished from their wedding breakfast, and he consults Holmes about her disappearance.
snapshots.why: Newspaper extracts (27–43) establish the vanished bride; safe recap.

snapshots.body: Second son of the Duke of Balmoral. His bride, Hatty Doran, left the wedding breakfast because she was already secretly married to Francis Hay Moulton, whom she had believed dead.
snapshots.why: Hatty’s account (204–207) explains the disappearance; his cold response follows at 210–215 but the reveal of the marriage is complete at 207.

snapshots.body: Second son of the Duke of Balmoral. His bride, Hatty Doran, left the wedding breakfast because she was already secretly married to Francis Hay Moulton, whom she had believed dead. He shakes her hand coldly, refuses Holmes’s invitation to supper and leaves.

entities.notes: Bare 'St. Simon' is NOT an alias: it appears inside sibling names and in 'St. Simon marriage case' (143). Counts include named aliases plus listed rules (approx.). Subtitle uses 'second son of the Duke of Balmoral' (text, 20/23).

entities.name: Hatty Doran
entities.subtitle: American heiress; only daughter of Aloysius Doran
entities.body: The only daughter of a Californian mining millionaire, newly married to Lord St. Simon. Society papers describe her as a fascinating heiress with a large dowry.

aliasRules.why: Holmes addresses her by this name after the reveal at 197; binding at 202 is after the gate.

snapshots.body: The only daughter of a Californian mining millionaire. She vanished from her own wedding breakfast after marrying Lord St. Simon; the papers report rumours of foul play.
snapshots.why: Newspaper accounts (27–39) report the disappearance.

snapshots.body: The only daughter of a Californian mining millionaire. She vanished from her own wedding breakfast after marrying Lord St. Simon and was seen entering Hyde Park with Flora Millar. Her wedding dress, shoes, wreath and veil have been found floating in the Serpentine.

snapshots.name: Hatty Doran (Mrs. Moulton)
snapshots.body: The missing bride reappears at Baker Street, introduced by Holmes as Mrs. Francis Hay Moulton; Holmes says Lord St. Simon has already met her.
snapshots.why: 197 introduces her as Mrs. Francis Hay Moulton.

snapshots.name: Hatty Doran (Mrs. Moulton)
snapshots.body: Before meeting Lord St. Simon she had secretly married Frank Moulton in San Francisco, then believed him killed by Apaches. Seeing him alive in the church on her wedding day, she slipped away from the breakfast to join him.
snapshots.why: 204–207: her own account of the prior marriage and her flight.

entities.notes: 'Lady St. Simon' (96,105,149,166,177) is bound to her; 177 ('Lady St. Simon is a myth') is Holmes’s hint, binding is harmless because the card stays pre-reveal until 197. 'Lady Clara St. Simon' is a different person (longer match). Many generic references ('the bride', 'my wife', 'the lady') left unbound.

entities.name: Francis Hay Moulton
entities.subtitle: American gentleman brought to Baker Street by Holmes
entities.body: An American gentleman whom Holmes brings to Baker Street on the evening of the case to meet Lord St. Simon.

aliasRules.why: Hatty’s name for him; all occurrences follow his introduction at 197.
Narration, him.
Narration, him.
Narration, him.

snapshots.body: An American gentleman introduced by Holmes, together with his wife, to Lord St. Simon. Holmes says Lord St. Simon has already met the lady.
snapshots.why: 197: 'Mr. and Mrs. Francis Hay Moulton'.

snapshots.body: Hatty Doran’s first love from a Rocky Mountain mining camp. They secretly married in San Francisco before he left to make his fortune.
snapshots.why: 204: Hatty’s account of the secret marriage.

snapshots.body: Hatty Doran’s husband by an earlier secret marriage. Reported killed by Apaches, he had been a prisoner, escaped and followed her to London; he was the man in the front pew who slipped her a note, and she left the wedding breakfast to join him.
snapshots.why: 205–207: reported death, the church, the note, the escape.

entities.notes: GATE: his identity is the solution. The 'gentleman in the pew' (91–95, 'a man' in 92 M), 'an American' in Holmes’s reasoning (219) before/around his reasoning, and the 'F. H. M.' initials (166) must NOT be bound to him before 197. Frank count: O=19, M=20.

entities.name: F. H. M.
entities.subtitle: Initials signing a note found in the bride’s dress
entities.body: Initials signing a note found in a card-case in the bride’s soaked wedding dress: ‘You will see me when all is ready. Come at once.’ Lestrade believes they stand for Flora Millar.

snapshots.name: F. H. M. (Francis Hay Moulton)
snapshots.body: The initials of Francis Hay Moulton, who scribbled the note in church and slipped it into Hatty’s hand when he returned her bouquet. Lestrade had taken them for Flora Millar’s.
snapshots.why: 197 gives his full name; 206 Hatty explains he wrote the note.

entities.notes: Separate entity so the initials are never bound to Moulton before the reveal. Body attributes the Flora reading to Lestrade.

entities.name: Flora Millar
entities.subtitle: Former danseuse at the Allegro; longtime friend of Lord St. Simon
entities.body: A former dancer at the Allegro who has known Lord St. Simon for years. She made a disturbance at the wedding breakfast, and the papers report that the police have arrested her.

snapshots.body: A former dancer at the Allegro and Lord St. Simon’s close friend of many years. She tried to force her way into the wedding breakfast and was seen with the bride in Hyde Park; Lestrade suspects she lured the bride into a trap and believes a note signed ‘F. H. M.’ proves it.
snapshots.why: 111–117 and 162–166 develop the police suspicion.

snapshots.body: A former dancer at the Allegro and Lord St. Simon’s close friend of many years. The bride’s own account shows she left to join Frank Moulton. The woman who accosted her in the Park with talk about Lord St. Simon, presumably Flora, had nothing to do with it, which undoes Lestrade’s theory and his reading of the ‘F. H. M.’ note.
snapshots.why: 206–207: the note came from Moulton; the bride left of her own will.

entities.notes: Arrest is reported at 39 (as 'the woman who had caused the original disturbance') before her first named mention at 43, so the first card may mention it. 'the woman, whose name has not been ascertained' (39) and 'Some woman' (207) left unbound: 39 is identified only at 43, and 207 is never explicitly named. 'Miss Millar' only in modern-en 164.

entities.name: Aloysius Doran
entities.subtitle: Hatty Doran’s father; Californian mining millionaire
entities.body: Hatty Doran’s father, said to be the richest man on the Pacific slope after striking gold. He has taken a furnished house at Lancaster Gate for the wedding.

aliasRules.why: Hatty’s name for her father in her narrative.

entities.notes: 'Pa' O=9, M=10. Generic 'her father' left unbound.

entities.name: Alice
entities.subtitle: Hatty Doran’s American maid
entities.body: Hatty Doran’s maid, an American who came with her from California.

aliasRules.why: In these paragraphs 'maid' denotes Hatty’s maid only (39 O/M, 110 O also mentions 'maid' but is covered by 'Alice' in the same phrase).

snapshots.body: Hatty Doran’s maid, an American who came with her from California. Lord St. Simon saw the bride talking with her after the wedding and thinks she is allowed too many liberties.
Hatty Doran’s American maid from California. She had known Frank Moulton there and was his friend; on the wedding day Hatty told her everything and had her pack a few things and ready her ulster.
snapshots.why: 207: Hatty’s account of the maid’s part.

entities.notes: Id chosen to avoid clashing with other Alices in the book. 'Alicia' (Lady Alicia Whittington, 39) does not match 'Alice' by word boundary. Name first given at 99. If the compiler prefers named-first binding, drop 39 from the maid rule. 110 O 'this maid, Alice' — 'maid' could also be added there (O only).

entities.name: The Duke of Balmoral
entities.subtitle: Lord St. Simon’s father
entities.body: Lord St. Simon’s father, once Secretary for Foreign Affairs. A society paper reports that he has had to sell his pictures in recent years.

aliasRules.why: Bare 'the Duke' in these paragraphs is Lord St. Simon’s father.

entities.notes: Never called 'St. Simon' in the text; only Lord St. Simon and his siblings carry that name.

entities.name: The Duchess of Balmoral
entities.subtitle: Wife of the Duke of Balmoral
entities.body: The Duke of Balmoral’s wife, one of the few guests at Lord St. Simon’s quiet wedding at St. George’s, Hanover Square.
entities.notes: Text never explicitly states she is Lord St. Simon’s mother (207 'his mother' is present at the breakfast), so the card does not assert it.

entities.name: Lord Backwater
entities.subtitle: Friend who recommended Holmes to Lord St. Simon
entities.body: A nobleman who told Lord St. Simon he could rely on Holmes. He attended the wedding, and the honeymoon was to be spent at his place near Petersfield.

entities.name: Lord Eustace St. Simon
entities.subtitle: Lord St. Simon’s younger brother
entities.body: Lord St. Simon’s younger brother, a guest at the wedding.
entities.notes: Text reads 'Lord Eustace and Lady Clara St. Simon'; only 'Lord Eustace' is bindable to him.

entities.name: Lady Clara St. Simon
entities.subtitle: Lord St. Simon’s younger sister
entities.body: Lord St. Simon’s younger sister, a guest at the wedding.
entities.notes: Longer match prevents the 'St. Simon' portion being claimed by anyone else.

entities.name: Lady Alicia Whittington
entities.subtitle: Guest at the St. Simon wedding
entities.body: One of the handful of guests at Lord St. Simon’s quiet wedding.
entities.notes: Not the maid Alice.

entities.name: The King of Scandinavia
entities.subtitle: Former client of Holmes
entities.body: A king whom Holmes names as his previous client in a delicate case of this sort; he declines to say more.
entities.notes: TRAP: not the King of Bohemia (king-of-bohemia). 'a king' at 50 left unbound.

entities.name: Alexander Holder
entities.subtitle: Senior partner of the bankers Holder & Stevenson
entities.body: A prominent London banker, senior partner in the City’s second-largest private bank, Holder & Stevenson of Threadneedle Street. He arrives at Baker Street in a state of frantic distress.

aliasRules.why: Narration naming the banker as he introduces himself.
Narration: Holder’s second visit.
Narration/tags; only Holder is called the banker. In 105 (original) the phrase sits in ‘the banker’s son’ and still denotes Holder.
Sentence-initial narration about Holder.
Narration: Fairbank is Holder’s residence.
Narration: Holder returns to Baker Street.
Narration: Holder on the train.
Narration: Holder seizes the recovered stones.
Holmes/Watson about Holder’s appointment; Holder seizes the stones (191 original).
Holmes about Holder’s appointment.
Arthur and Mary addressing Holder.
Arthur and Mary addressing Holder (modern rendering of ‘dad’).
Narration: Mary goes to Holder.
Mary speaking of Holder.
Mary speaking of Holder (original has bare ‘uncle’s’, left unbound).
Mary refers to Holder; matches the modern binding.

snapshots.body: A prominent London banker who accepted the Beryl Coronet as security for a £50,000 loan to an illustrious client and took it home to Streatham. After catching his son Arthur with the damaged coronet at night, he handed him to the police and has come to Holmes for help.
snapshots.why: 11:79 completes Holder’s account: the damage, the missing beryls and Arthur’s arrest.

snapshots.body: A prominent London banker who accepted the Beryl Coronet as security for a loan to an illustrious client. Holmes recovered the three missing stones for him, showed that Arthur had been wrongly accused, and told him that his niece Mary had fled with Sir George Burnwell.
snapshots.why: 11:190–220 resolve the case for Holder.

entities.notes: Bare ‘Holder’ never stands alone in either edition; every instance is inside ‘Mr. Holder’, ‘Alexander Holder’, ‘Miss (Mary) Holder’ or the firm name ‘Holder & Stevenson’, so no bare-surname alias is needed. Holder narrates 11:17–79 in the first person; his ‘my client’ there means the illustrious client, not himself.

entities.name: Arthur Holder
entities.subtitle: Alexander Holder’s only son
entities.body: Alexander Holder’s only son, whom his father admits to having spoiled. Charming but wild, he has run up gambling debts through an aristocratic club and the influence of his friend Sir George Burnwell.

aliasRules.why: Holder speaking of Arthur (39 is modern only).
Holder speaking of Arthur.
Holmes speaking to Holder about Arthur (several only in the original).

snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s only son, with gambling debts and a worldly friend in Sir George Burnwell. His father found him at night holding the damaged Beryl Coronet with three beryls missing; Arthur refused to explain and was taken into police custody.
snapshots.why: 11:65–79: Holder catches Arthur with the coronet and gives him into custody.

snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s only son, arrested after his father found him with the damaged Beryl Coronet. Holmes has told Holder that Arthur did not take the stones and that he is owed a humble apology.
snapshots.why: 11:196–198: Holmes declares Arthur innocent.

snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s only son, wrongly arrested over the damaged Beryl Coronet. He had seen his cousin Mary hand the coronet out of a window, chased Sir George Burnwell down the lane and wrestled it back, minus one fragment. He stayed silent to protect Mary’s secret.
snapshots.why: 11:207–210: Holmes reconstructs what Arthur actually did.

entities.notes: The surname Holder is never attached to Arthur in the text; it follows from his being Alexander Holder’s son. Display name uses it for clarity. The police and his father treat him as the thief until 11:198; keep that attributed.

entities.name: Mary Holder
entities.subtitle: Alexander Holder’s niece and adopted daughter
entities.body: Alexander Holder’s niece, whom he adopted when her father died five years ago and treats as a daughter. She runs his household and has twice refused Arthur’s proposals of marriage.

aliasRules.why: Holder introducing Mary.
Holder speaking of Mary.
Holder speaking of Mary.
Holmes speaking to Holder of Mary.
Holmes speaking to Holder of Mary.
Holmes: Arthur’s cousin = Mary.
Holmes to Holder about Mary.

snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s niece and adopted daughter, who ran his household. She has left Fairbank overnight, leaving a note saying she brought trouble on her uncle and begging him not to search for her.
snapshots.why: 11:179–183: Mary’s disappearance and farewell note.

snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s niece and adopted daughter. Holmes reveals that she had a secret understanding with Sir George Burnwell and has fled with him.
snapshots.why: 11:202: Holmes names the understanding and the flight.

snapshots.body: Alexander Holder’s niece and adopted daughter. Persuaded by her secret lover Sir George Burnwell, she took the Beryl Coronet from her uncle’s bureau at night and handed it out of the hall window to him. She has since fled with him.
snapshots.why: 11:206–207: Holmes describes Mary taking the coronet and passing it out of the window.

entities.notes: First-mention text in both editions is ‘my little Mary’ / ‘My little Mary’ (11:39). The young woman who enters at 11:106 is left unbound until she is named at 11:118. ‘MARY’ is her signature on the farewell note (11:183).

entities.name: Sir George Burnwell
entities.subtitle: Arthur Holder’s worldly older friend
entities.body: Arthur’s older friend, a handsome, much-travelled man of the world and a brilliant talker, whose influence keeps drawing Arthur back to gambling. Holder finds him fascinating in person but says his cynicism makes him distrust him.

aliasRules.why: Holmes’s nickname for the booted man’s tracks; by 11:208 the reader has been told this man was Sir George.

snapshots.body: Arthur’s worldly older friend and a frequent visitor at Holder’s house. Holmes reveals that he had a secret understanding with Holder’s niece Mary and that the two have fled together.
snapshots.why: 11:202 reveals the understanding and flight.

snapshots.body: Arthur’s worldly older friend, whom Holmes calls a ruined gambler and one of the most dangerous men in England. He received the Beryl Coronet from Mary at the hall window; Arthur chased him down the lane, cut him over the eye and wrested the coronet back, leaving a fragment in his hands.
snapshots.why: 11:204–208: Holmes’s account of his character and the struggle in the lane.

snapshots.body: Arthur’s worldly older friend, who took the Beryl Coronet with Mary’s help and fled with her. Holmes traced him by his boots and held him at pistol-point. Burnwell admitted he had already sold the three stones for £600. In return for a promise of no prosecution he gave up the receiver’s address, and Holmes bought the stones back from the receiver for £1,000 each.
snapshots.why: 11:216–219: identification and confrontation.

entities.notes: Called simply ‘Sir George’ in modern 11:39, 208 and in both editions at 11:217 (‘Sir George’s house’). His guilt is gated: first card reflects only Holder’s wary description at 11:38–39. The ‘dark figure’ (11:208) and ‘someone in the gloom’ (11:207) are left unbound.

entities.name: Lucy Parr
entities.subtitle: Second waiting-maid in the Holder household
entities.body: The Holders’ second waiting-maid, in service only a few months but with excellent references. She is very pretty and has admirers who sometimes hang about the house.

snapshots.body: The Holders’ second waiting-maid, in service only a few months. She brought in the coffee on the evening Holder spoke of the coronet; he believes she had left the room, but Mary suggests she may have overheard him. That night Mary saw her slipping back in at the kitchen door after meeting her sweetheart, the greengrocer Francis Prosper.
snapshots.why: 11:42, 56–58 and 126–133 give her movements, her sweetheart’s name (133) and Mary’s suggestion (attributed).

snapshots.body: The Holders’ second waiting-maid. Holmes confirmed from the snow and from inquiry that her night outing was simply a meeting with her sweetheart at the kitchen door, and ruled out the maids as the coronet’s takers.
snapshots.why: 11:212 confirms the meeting; 11:215 excludes the maids.

entities.notes: The waiting-maid is referred to generically (‘the maid’, ‘one of the servants’, ‘this girl’) at 11:126–130 and 11:206; those are left unbound.

entities.name: Francis Prosper
entities.subtitle: Greengrocer who delivers to the Holder house
entities.body: The greengrocer who brings the Holders their vegetables. Mary saw him in the dark at the kitchen door with the maid Lucy Parr on the night of the theft.

aliasRules.why: Holmes’s nickname for the man with the wooden leg whose tracks he read at the kitchen door; same paragraph confirms it was the maid’s sweetheart.

snapshots.body: The greengrocer who delivers to the Holders and Lucy Parr’s sweetheart. Holmes guessed his wooden leg from the tracks at the kitchen door, and confirmed that he and Lucy had only met there to talk.
snapshots.why: 11:136 (wooden leg) and 11:212 (tracks and inquiry confirm the meeting).

entities.notes: The wooden leg is Holmes’s deduction at 11:136, kept out of the first card. Modern 11:212 renders ‘Wooden-leg’ as ‘The man with the wooden leg’ (unbound).

entities.name: The illustrious client
entities.subtitle: Exalted borrower who pledged the Beryl Coronet
entities.body: A visitor bearing ‘one of the highest, noblest, most exalted names in England’, whom Holder declines to name even to Holmes. He borrows £50,000 from Holder’s bank and leaves the Beryl Coronet as security, promising to reclaim it on Monday.

aliasRules.why: Holder’s narrative: ‘my client’ here is the exalted borrower, not Holder.

aliasRules.alias: one who was far greater than I
aliasRules.why: Holder pleading with Arthur about the client’s honour.
Holder pleading with Arthur about the client’s honour.

entities.notes: Never named or identified in the text; must not be identified. Pronoun ‘he’ in 11:18–33 left unbound.

entities.name: Violet Hunter
entities.subtitle: A London governess; Holmes’s client in this story
entities.body: A young governess with no family to advise her, who writes to Holmes asking whether she should accept a strangely well-paid position in Hampshire.

aliasRules.why: Watson calls Miss Hunter ‘our client’ as she replies to Holmes; unambiguous.
Standalone signature of her telegram. Elsewhere uppercase HUNTER is inside the longer ‘VIOLET HUNTER’ (11) or ‘MISS HUNTER’ (62, original only).

snapshots.body: She took the post at the Copper Beeches, where the Rucastles had her wear an electric-blue dress and sit with her back to the window, and she found a locked, barricaded wing. Frightened by Rucastle’s threats, she has summoned Holmes to Winchester.
snapshots.why: 157 ends her account of events at the house and her reason for wiring Holmes.

snapshots.body: She locked Mrs. Toller in the cellar and gave Holmes the keys to the locked wing, though the prisoner had already gone. Watson later reports that she became head of a private school at Walsall, with considerable success.
snapshots.why: 211 gives her later career.

entities.notes: Introduced by signature in her letter (11); appears in person at 18 and is named ‘Miss Hunter’ at 20. ‘Miss Hunter’ is O18/M19 because modern-en 62 writes ‘Dear Miss Hunter’ where original-en has ‘DEAR MISS HUNTER’. Generic ‘a young lady’ (18), ‘his new client’ (21), ‘the young lady’ (104) left unbound.

entities.name: Jephro Rucastle
entities.subtitle: Owner of the Copper Beeches near Winchester
entities.body: A very stout, smiling Hampshire gentleman who offers Violet Hunter an unusually high salary to be governess to his young son, on condition that she cut her hair short and humour his wife’s little whims.

aliasRules.why: Only bare ‘Rucastle’ occurrences not preceded by Mr./Mrs./Miss/Alice; both are ‘Rucastle’s’ and denote Jephro. Bare ‘Rucastle’ must not be a global alias (namesake trap).
Holmes has just asked him ‘where’s your daughter?’ (187), so the fat man is plainly Rucastle; no spoiler.

snapshots.body: Holmes now believes Rucastle hired Violet Hunter to impersonate his daughter, Alice, whom he suspects is locked in the barricaded room rather than in America, and that the window performances were meant to deceive the man watching from the road.
snapshots.why: 169: Holmes’s deduction (attributed).

snapshots.body: Holmes believes Rucastle has been keeping his daughter Alice prisoner. Confronted by Holmes at the door of the empty room, Rucastle rushed downstairs — Violet Hunter cried that he had gone for the dog — but his starving mastiff seized him instead. Watson shot it, and Rucastle was carried inside alive but badly mauled.
snapshots.why: 186–194: confrontation and the dog’s attack.

snapshots.body: Mrs. Toller confirms that he kept his daughter Alice prisoner to stop her marrying and taking control of money left to her by will, and hired Violet Hunter to drive away her suitor, Mr. Fowler. His own half-starved mastiff, loosed that evening, mauled him.
snapshots.why: 201–205: Mrs. Toller’s account and Holmes’s summary, confirmed by her.

snapshots.body: He kept his daughter Alice prisoner for her money and was mauled by his own mastiff. He survived as a broken man, cared for by his devoted wife, and still lives with his old servants.
snapshots.why: 211: final outcome.

entities.notes: He appears unnamed from 24 (‘A prodigiously stout man’ / ‘An enormously stout man’) through 59 at the agency; his name is first given by his letter’s signature at 63. Those descriptions, ‘the gentleman’ (35, 60), ‘my employer’ (112, 119, 132), ‘the father’ (42), ‘the man’ (157) and ‘a very fat and burly man’ (186) are left unbound. Binding the agency description at 24 would not spoil the mystery, but it would show his name 39 paragraphs before the text gives it, so it is left as a reviewer choice. Counts: JEPHRO RUCASTLE 1 + Jephro 1 + Mr. Rucastle 19 + bare Rucastle 2 + The fat man 1.

entities.name: Mrs. Rucastle
entities.subtitle: Jephro Rucastle’s second wife
entities.body: Rucastle’s pale, silent wife, much younger than he is, devoted to her husband and little son. Violet Hunter is told the job’s odd requests are her wishes.

snapshots.body: After her husband was mauled by the mastiff, she nursed him; Watson reports that he survived as a broken man, kept alive only by her care.
snapshots.why: 211: outcome.

entities.notes: Referred to earlier only as ‘my wife’ (44, 53, 62) and ‘his wife’ (70): unbound. ‘Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle’ (109, 118, 143, 157) binds only the ‘Mrs. Rucastle’ span to her; ‘Mr.’ alone stays unbound. The text never states how much she knew of the imprisonment, so the card does not say. At 70 Violet and Holmes speculate that she might be mad; she is not (112), so the card avoids that suggestion.

entities.name: Alice Rucastle
entities.subtitle: Jephro Rucastle’s daughter by his first marriage
entities.body: Rucastle’s grown daughter. In his letter he says she is now in Philadelphia, and Violet Hunter is to wear a dress that belonged to her.

snapshots.body: Rucastle says she went to Philadelphia because she disliked her stepmother. Holmes now believes she never left: he thinks she is the prisoner in the barricaded room, and that Violet was hired to impersonate her.
snapshots.why: 169: Holmes identifies the prisoner by deduction (attributed).

snapshots.body: Mrs. Toller confirms that Alice’s father imprisoned her. A will gave her money, and he wanted it kept from her suitor, Mr. Fowler. When she refused to sign it over, his pressure brought on brain-fever, and her hair was cut off during the illness.
snapshots.why: 201–203: Mrs. Toller’s account; imprisonment confirmed at 203.

snapshots.body: She escaped through the skylight with Mr. Fowler’s help. They married by special licence in Southampton the next day, and he now holds a government post in Mauritius.
snapshots.why: 206–211: escape explained, then the marriage.

entities.notes: GATE: her presence in the locked room is the story’s mystery. Never bind ‘the prisoner’ (180), ‘the real person’ (169), the shadow or footsteps (144), ‘his victim’ (181) or ‘the poor girl’ (171) to her before 169; they are left unbound throughout. ‘the daughter’ (112, 169) and ‘your daughter’ (187) are also unbound. Counts: Alice@62 + Miss Alice Rucastle@169 + Miss Rucastle@169,211 + Miss Alice@200,201×2 = 7.

entities.name: Edward
entities.subtitle: The Rucastles’ young son
entities.body: The Rucastles’ six-year-old son and Violet Hunter’s charge: a spoiled, ill-tempered child, small for his age, who delights in hurting small creatures.
entities.notes: Named only once (‘little Edward’, 118). Otherwise ‘one child’ (41), ‘the child’, ‘little son’ (113), ‘my charge’ (137): unbound. Holmes calls the child’s cruelty the gravest point (169, 171), but that is an interpretation, not a plot fact about him.

entities.name: The Rucastles
entities.subtitle: The family at the Copper Beeches
entities.body: Jephro Rucastle and his wife, Violet Hunter’s employers at the Copper Beeches near Winchester.
entities.notes: Used at 135, 161, 167 and 184 for the couple. Kept separate from the individual cards because bare ‘Rucastle’ is a namesake trap.

entities.name: Toller
entities.subtitle: Groom and manservant at the Copper Beeches
entities.body: The Rucastles’ manservant — a rough, uncouth man with grizzled hair and whiskers who smells of drink and has twice been drunk since Violet Hunter arrived. His wife is the household’s only other servant.

snapshots.body: The Rucastles’ rough, grizzled manservant and groom, often drunk, and the only one who can manage the mastiff, Carlo, which he lets loose at night.
snapshots.why: Carlo and the nightly release introduced at 12:132.

snapshots.body: He was so drunk that night that Violet Hunter could take his keys. Holmes concludes that Mr. Fowler, by winning over Toller’s wife, made sure Toller never lacked drink.
snapshots.why: 208: Holmes’s summary, confirmed by Mrs. Toller at 209.

entities.notes: Bare ‘Toller’ only; ‘Mrs. Toller’ (longer) goes to his wife and ‘Tollers’ to the couple. Modern-en 143 names Toller twice where the original uses ‘him’, so the counts differ by one. ‘An elderly man with a red face’ (192) is Toller, named at 194; left unbound though binding it would not spoil anything. His wife at 115, 143 and 160 (‘his wife’) is unbound.

entities.name: Mrs. Toller
entities.subtitle: Toller’s wife; servant at the Copper Beeches
entities.body: Toller’s wife, the Rucastles’ other servant: a very tall, strong, sour-faced woman, as silent as her mistress.

snapshots.body: Released from the cellar by Rucastle, she tells Holmes the whole story. She calls herself Miss Alice’s friend and confirms that Mr. Fowler won her over and arranged the ladder for Alice’s escape.
snapshots.why: 200–209: her account; 209 confirms Holmes’s summary.

entities.notes: Described earlier as ‘His wife’ (115), ‘his wife’ (143, 160) and later ‘a tall, gaunt woman’ (194): all unbound. The Holmes quote ‘knows more about this matter than anyone else’ (197) is not a spoiler.

entities.name: The Tollers
entities.subtitle: The servant couple at the Copper Beeches
entities.body: Toller and his wife, the Rucastles’ only servants.
entities.notes: One occurrence (‘the quarters of the Tollers’ / ‘the Tollers’ quarters’, 136). It could be left unbound if one-mention family entries are not wanted.

entities.name: Carlo
entities.subtitle: The Rucastles’ mastiff
entities.body: Rucastle’s huge, half-starved mastiff, kept chained in an outhouse by day and let loose by Toller at night to guard the grounds.

aliasRules.why: Rucastle’s threat ‘throw you to the mastiff’; 132 already binds ‘Carlo’ directly.
Each denotes Carlo. Not global: at 62 ‘the dog’ matches inside ‘the dog-cart’.
Holmes: ‘The dog is let loose at night’.

exclude.why: Part of ‘the dog-cart’, a carriage; the hyphen makes a word boundary.

snapshots.body: Left unfed for two days and set loose, it seized Rucastle by the throat. Watson shot it dead.
snapshots.why: 192–194: the attack and its death.

entities.notes: Counts: Carlo 1 + mastiff@156 1 + the dog@157,190,193 3 + The dog@169 1 = 6. Also ‘a large animal’ (129), ‘a giant dog’ (133), ‘the savage creature’ (157) and ‘the huge famished brute’ (194): unbound.

entities.name: Mr. Fowler
entities.subtitle: Alice Rucastle’s suitor
entities.body: The young man who met Alice Rucastle at a friend’s house and stayed loyal to her through her long illness.

snapshots.name: Mr. Fowler
snapshots.body: Mrs. Toller confirms Holmes’s account. Fowler, a persistent seaman, kept watch on the house, won her over with gifts, kept her husband supplied with drink, and had a ladder ready to rescue Alice once Rucastle went out.
snapshots.why: 206–209: Holmes’s summary, confirmed at 209.

snapshots.body: He rescued Alice Rucastle from her father’s house and married her by special licence in Southampton the next day. He now holds a government appointment in Mauritius.
snapshots.why: 211: outcome.

entities.notes: Named only from 201. His earlier appearances as the watcher on the road belong to the separate ‘man-in-the-road’ entity, which is never bound to him before the reveal. ‘her young man’ (201) is unbound. ‘seaman’ in the subtitle comes from 206; this is an ordinary occupation and spoils nothing.

entities.name: The man in the road
entities.subtitle: A watcher on the Southampton road
entities.body: A small, bearded man in a grey suit who leans on the railings by the road and stares up at the house while Violet Hunter sits laughing in the window.

aliasRules.alias: a small bearded man in a grey suit
aliasRules.why: First sighting, in Violet’s mirror.

aliasRules.alias: a small, bearded man in a grey suit
aliasRules.why: Modern-en wording of the first sighting.
Mrs. Rucastle refers to the same watcher.
Modern-en wording.

snapshots.body: Holmes believes he is a friend of the Rucastles’ daughter, possibly her fiancé, and that Violet’s laughter and wave were staged to convince him that the daughter no longer wanted him.

snapshots.name: The man in the road (Mr. Fowler)
snapshots.body: The watcher was Mr. Fowler, Alice Rucastle’s suitor, who kept the house under watch until he could rescue her.
snapshots.why: 206: Holmes says Fowler ‘blockaded the house’; Mrs. Toller confirms at 209.

entities.notes: Concealed identity: must stay a separate entity from mr-fowler until after 209. A compiler could alternatively bind these spans to mr-fowler, but only with a first card that hides the name; a separate entity is safer.

entities.name: Miss Stoper
entities.subtitle: Manager of Westaway’s governess agency
entities.body: She manages Westaway’s, a well-known West End agency for governesses, where Violet Hunter calls each week in search of a post.

aliasRules.why: Clearly Miss Stoper.
Modern-en lowercase.

entities.notes: Violet suspects (56) that her refusal cost Miss Stoper a commission. That is Violet’s suspicion, so it is left out of the card.

entities.name: Colonel Spence Munro
entities.subtitle: Violet Hunter’s former employer
entities.body: The army officer whose children Violet Hunter taught for five years, until he took up an appointment in Halifax, Nova Scotia, and took his family to America.
entities.notes: Mentioned only (22, 31). ‘the colonel’ (22) is unbound.
